# I0716 Dossier: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data

Research date: 2026-10-13. Evidence quality is tagged: [P] primary or peer-reviewed or regulator, [V] vendor claim, [I] my inference or arithmetic.

## 1. Verdict

**Do not pursue as pitched. Pursue only as a narrow, services-led wedge, and only after a price test.** The problem is well documented. The "AI agents" part of the why-now is weaker than the pitch implies, and the white space is smaller than the earlier competitor pass concluded. Three findings drive this:

- A major analytics firm (SSRS) already productized the core mechanism, a parallel probability sample used as ground truth.
- A new independent audit firm launched a month ago.
- Every price anchor I found is far below $3-15k per study.

| Dimension | Score (1-5) | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Problem severity | 4 | Pew, the YouGov retraction and an industry benchmark all show it |
| Why-now | 3 | Narrative tailwind is real, but AI-agent prevalence in live traffic is unproven |
| White space | 2 | SSRS, Data Quality Co-op (DQC) and Signals & Standards overlap |
| Willingness to pay | 2 | No evidence of anyone paying for per-study audits, and no mandate |
| Market size | 2 | My estimate is $10-25M a year serviceable |
| Defensibility | 2 | The control sample is rentable, and trust is the real moat |

## 2. Is the problem real? Yes, and it is mostly human fraud

- Pew (Aug 2026, n=11,114 opt-in respondents) flagged 18% as bogus via trap questions. CloudResearch's Sentry would have excluded nearly half. Trap questions and Sentry performed about the same. [P] https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2026/08/27/no-easy-fix-for-bogus-respondents-in-online-opt-in-polls/
  - Voter-file matching removed 64% of respondents and worsened bias. The primacy effect rose to +14 from +9 unscreened.
  - Self-reported turnout was 84% unscreened against a validated benchmark of about 77%. The screens moved it the wrong way, to 85-87%.
  - The presidential vote went from tied to a 3-7 point Harris lead depending on the screen. Pew says every method modestly raised overestimation of Democratic support.
  - This supports the idea's claim that "remove the flagged" is itself a bias source.
- YouGov and the Bible Society withdrew the "Quiet Revival" church-attendance report (April 2026) after YouGov found fraudulent respondents in the 2024 data. [P] https://www.research-live.com/article/news/yougov-church-attendance-report-withdrawn-due-to-fraudulent-responses/id/5148193
  - The Bible Society said it had "repeatedly sought and received assurances" from the vendor.
  - YouGov said its anti-fraud measures "were not administered effectively".
  - This is the idea's exact scenario: the seller scored itself and the buyer had no referee. The buyer's remedy was to ask the vendor again, not to hire an auditor.
- The Global Data Quality (GDQ) H1 2026 benchmark covers about 1.8M records from 46 companies. [P] https://www.research-live.com/article/news/survey-removal-rates-remain-high/id/5150456
  - Pre- and in-survey removal was 28.5% for agencies and 21.2% for suppliers, with a further 8.9-10.7% removed post-survey.
  - B2B post-survey removal was 59.6%.
  - Of 151 sample buyers, 43% of B2B buyers were dissatisfied.
- Op4G/SliceMR and SNWare were federally indicted (April 2025) over survey-data fraud. [P] https://www.insightsassociation.org/News/Industry-News/ArticleID/1651/Insights-Association-Issues-Statement-Regarding-Federal-Indictments-of-Op4G-SliceMR-and-SNWare-Research
  - The Insights Association (IA) noted its ISO 27001 audit would not have caught the alleged conduct. Existing certifications do not test whether data are real.
- Kantar claims post-field rejection rates rose about 300% in three years. [V] https://www.kantar.com/inspiration/ai/is-panel-fraud-the-new-ad-fraud

## 3. Why-now check: partly real, partly overstated

**Real:**

- Westwood's PNAS agent evaded detection 99.8% of the time. As few as 10-52 fake responses would have flipped seven 2024 national polls, at about five cents per fake response. [P] https://www.404media.co/a-researcher-made-an-ai-that-completely-breaks-the-online-surveys-scientists-rely-on/
- AAPOR released a Task Force report on AI on 5/8/2026 and proposed Code revisions. [P] https://aapor.org/announcements/task-force-on-responsible-ai-integration-in-survey-research-report/
- NORC's April 2026 review cites 15-30% industry fraud rates. [P] https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdf2026/cpss-research-brief-fraud-lit-review.pdf

**Overstated:**

- The agent was purpose-built by academics. A critique preprint says the PNAS papers claim field-level vulnerability without benchmarks or reproducible real-world impact. Its author note says PNAS rejected it on 22 May 2026. [P] https://sciety.org/articles/activity/10.31235/osf.io/ykxwj_v1
- Prolific's CEO reports agent detection "at or below 1%" on every platform except MTurk (about 5,200 participants, 10 platforms). [V] https://www.prolific.com/resources/ai-agent-debate-open-letter-by-ceo-phelim-bradley
- CloudResearch says click farms, not AI, are the dominant threat today. [V] https://www.cloudresearch.com/resources/blog/bot-olympics-50k-challenge-ai-agents-survey-fraud/
- I could not verify a secondhand claim that agents are under 0.1% of CloudResearch traffic.
- The Bot Olympics has published no results yet, and CloudResearch is a sponsor.

**Implication [I]:** the defensible pitch is "opt-in panels carry 10-30% bad data and vendors grade themselves." That is true today. "AI agents beat attention checks" is a forward-looking risk.

## 4. Competitive landscape

| Player | What it does | Funding / traction | Overlap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SSRS** | Trains an isolation forest on a parallel probability-panel sample to flag bad opt-in responses, built into its Encipher hybrid blending. [P] https://ssrs.com/wp-content/uploads/How-Machine-Learning-and-a-Parallel-Probability-Sample-Can-Help-Detect-Bad-Data-in-Online-Opt-in-Samples.pdf | Established research firm. The brief reports about 9% of opt-in respondents failing 2+ checks against 1% or less in probability. | **Direct on mechanism.** Not neutral on sample, and it does not offer a per-study audit stamp. |
| **Signals & Standards Research Consulting** | Independent audit of insight firms' quality claims (processes and results), launched 9/11/2026 by a former Toluna, NPD and Circana chief research officer. [P] https://www.mrweb.com/drno/news40310.htm | Solo practice. No pricing or clients disclosed. | **Direct on neutrality and audit.** It has no control sample or calibration. |
| **Data Quality Co-op** | Clearinghouse with a 0-1000 Data Trust Score and vendor scorecards. Partnered with Advertiser Perceptions in 3/2026. [P] https://www.research-live.com/article/news/data-quality-coop-partners-with-advertising-intelligence-business/id/5148206 | $1.25M first round (Oct 2024). [P] https://www.utahbusiness.com/press-releases/2024/10/29/data-quality-coop-secures-125-million/ Pricing unpublished. | Direct on scorecards. |
| **Verasight** | Verified panel from $3.50 per complete. [V] https://verasight.io/self-serve-surveys It claims to beat Pew's opt-in samples on accuracy. | Funding undisclosed after several searches. | Owns the "known-real" asset but sells sample. |
| **Verisoul** | Entry-time bot and device detection. | $8.8M Series A (Dec 2025, High Alpha) plus $3.25M seed, 100+ customers, 6x revenue growth. [P] https://www.highalpha.com/news/verisoul-raises-8-8m-series-a-to-fight-fraud-fake-users-and-bots-in-the-ai-era SaaS at $99-350/month. [V] https://www.emporiaresearch.com/blog/a-buyers-guide-to-anti-fraud-tools-in-market-research-sampling | Adjacent. The earlier file's "$9M" is the rounded figure. |
| **Roundtable** | Behavioral "Proof of Human" API. | Y Combinator S23. [P] https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/roundtable Amount unverified. | Adjacent. |
| **CloudResearch, Prolific** | Detection plus their own sample. Prolific offers a "100% Human Guarantee" that refunds twice the response cost on a detected agent. [V] | Prolific's $32M raise (2023) is aggregator-sourced. | Adjacent. Both are conflicted, and both self-test. |
| **dtect, Obsurvant** | Entry detection (dtect) and quality profiling (Obsurvant). Both are vendor-claim only. | Undisclosed. | Adjacent. |
| **Pew, NORC** | Publish the method free. | Non-profit. | The method itself is free to copy. |
| **Simile, Aaru** | Synthetic respondents. Simile raised $200M at $2B (July 2026). [V] https://letsdatascience.com/news/simile-raises-200-million-for-consumer-ai-twins-43af6a77 | Heavily funded. | Substitute that could shrink panel spend. |

Prior art for independent supplier ranking: Lucid's Fulcrum Quality (2016) ranked about 20 suppliers quarterly. It was run by the sample platform, so it was not truly independent. [P] https://www.research-live.com/article/news/lucid-launches-sample-verification-programme/id/5011382

**Incumbents who could add this:**

- SSRS already has the mechanism.
- Ipsos KnowledgePanel and NORC AmeriSpeak hold the control asset.
- Cint (Q1 2026 net sales EUR 34.0m) sits on a quality-sensitive marketplace. [P] https://investors.cint.com/sites/cint/files/2026-04/Cint-Group-Q1-2026-presentation.pdf
- Qualtrics already gates its Expert Review fraud detection behind a license feature. https://www.qualtrics.com/support/survey-platform/survey-module/survey-checker/fraud-detection/

Only the neutrality part is hard for them. That is a reputation moat, not a technology moat.

## 5. Bottom-up market size

There is no clean sourced customer count. A single syndicated report puts online survey research at about $4.2B in 2025 [V, one source] https://trendxinsights.com/syndicated-market-research-reports/online-survey-research-market/. The estimates below use my assumptions.

| Segment | Assumption [I] | Annual revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Enterprise programs ($50-150k) | 150-300 insights organizations with $2M or more sample spend; 15-25% adopt; $100k average | $2-7M |
| High-stakes per-study audits ($10-30k) | 500-1,000 studies a year (litigation, pharma access and pricing, pollsters, publishers) at $15k average | $7-15M |
| Vendor scorecard subscriptions | DQC and Verisoul-style pricing of hundreds of dollars a month | Under $2M |
| **Total serviceable** | | **about $10-25M** |

This supports a 1-5 person boutique, not a venture-scale business. Dynata's 2024 Chapter 11 (debt cut from $1.3B to $780M) suggests sample economics are thin, so buyers' budgets are not generous. [P] https://hartfordbusiness.com/article/shelton-based-data-research-firm-emerges-from-bankruptcy-new-equity-owners-include-bain/

## 6. Willingness to pay: problem evidence is strong, payment evidence is thin

**Price anchors, all far below the proposed price:**

- Buyers balk at about $3 per complete, and some push for $2.75. A researcher says he would pay $5 instead of $2 but could not persuade clients. [V] https://www.greenbook.org/insights/research-methodologies/panel-quality-stinks-and-clients-are-to-blame
- A 1,000-complete study therefore costs about $3-5k in sample. A $3-15k audit would be 1-4 times the fieldwork bill. [I]
- Detection runs $99-350 a month (Verisoul). DQC's price is unpublished.
- A litigation consumer survey costs about $15-20k in total, and specialist audiences cost more. [P] https://calawyers.org/intellectual-property-law/event-recap-trademark-spotlight-trademark-surveys-litigation/

**Evidence in favor:**

- Emporia's buyer guide calls an extra independent check "an insurance policy" on critical studies. [V]
- Advertiser Perceptions partnered with DQC to add an "independent layer" of validation. The commercial terms are undisclosed.
- A credible veteran just opened an audit-only practice. That is a market signal, not revenue evidence.

**Missing:** I found no RFPs, no regulation mandating audits, and no public example of anyone paying $3-15k for a per-study audit. The earlier competitor pass found the same gap. Buyers' natural fix is switching suppliers. Prolific's own numbers are $8.26 per quality respondent from direct panels against $74.43 from marketplaces. [V]

## 7. Unit economics (my arithmetic, flagged assumptions)

**Renting the control is cheap:**

- n=500 at 10 minutes via Verasight costs about $1.75-2.5k at $3.50-5 per complete.
- Ipsos KnowledgePanel omnibus is $1,000 per question unit for units 1-5 and $750 after (2024 brochure). [P] https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/KP_Omnibus_Brochure_2024.pdf Fifteen units (n=1,000) cost about $12.5k.

**Building your own address-based panel is expensive and slow:**

- NORC's initial household response is about 6% using four mailings plus $5 prepaid and $25-50 postpaid incentives. [P] https://amerispeak.norc.org/content/dam/amerispeak/about-amerispeak/pdf/amerispeak-technical-overview.pdf
- A mailed teacher-panel experiment cost $67 per recruit at 27.5% response, rising to $106 with larger promised incentives. [P] https://www.surveypractice.org/article/17882-the-effect-of-incentives-and-mode-of-contact-on-the-recruitment-of-teachers-into-survey-panels/attachment/46679.html
- At a 6% yield, I infer several hundred dollars per recruit. That implies low-to-mid six figures for 2,000 verified humans, plus maintenance. The "first 30 days" plan of recruiting 2,000 humans is not realistic.
- 2,000 respondents also supports few subgroup estimates.

**Gross margin on one study [I]:**

- At a $10k price: control $2-5k, plus 25 analyst hours at $150 (about $3.75k), plus detection signals under $0.5k. That leaves roughly 8-38% margin.
- At a $3k price the audit loses money.
- The business only works at $10k or more per study, or as retainers.

**Substitution:** since a verified-human sample rents at $3.50-5, "scarce known-real reference" is overstated. A buyer can buy the clean sample itself.

## 8. Regulatory and liability landscape

- No regulator mandates third-party survey audits. I found only voluntary regimes:
  - ISO 20252 certification through the IA's CIRQ.
  - IA's pledge.
  - GDQ metrics.
  - AAPOR's proposed Code revisions.
- Courts usually admit surveys and treat flaws as going to weight, unless flaws are "fatal". [P] https://calawyers.org/intellectual-property-law/event-recap-trademark-spotlight-trademark-surveys-litigation/
  - In NetAirus v. Apple (C.D. Cal. 2013), a survey of respondents "with no basis" to answer was excluded. https://patentlaw.jmbm.com/2013/11/netairus-v-apple-district-cour.html
  - I found no ruling excluding a survey for bots or fraudulent panelists across two attempts. The litigation wedge from the earlier pass is therefore speculative.
- Liability for the auditor [I, not sourced]:
  - An "audit stamp" invites professional-liability exposure if a stamped study is later retracted.
  - Publishing vendor scorecards invites trade-libel and false-advertising claims from vendors.
  - Getting response-level paradata and device data from vendors raises contract and privacy limits.
  - Budget for E&O insurance and counsel-reviewed methodology.
- Pharma and healthcare-professional (HCP) panels have documented fake-HCP problems, but I found no quantified prevalence. https://www.m3globalresearch.com/blog/fake-surveys-healthcare-professionals/

## 9. Risks and kill criteria

1. **Price cliff.** Routine studies will not carry a multiple of their sample cost.
2. **Credibility cold start.** An audit sells trust, and the closest competitor is a 25-year veteran on IA and GDQ committees.
3. **Mechanism is copyable.** SSRS published the method, and Pew published the design.
4. **Threat may stay hypothetical.** If agents stay under 1% of live traffic, urgency fades. If synthetic respondents win, panel audit demand shrinks.
5. **Self-fix.** Panels adopt probability blending or "100% Human" guarantees, which removes the pain.

**Kill if** fewer than 3 of 10 insights heads will commit more than $10k for a single-study audit, or if no litigation survey expert will name a project where the audit mattered.

## 10. Recommended next step

If the owner still wants this idea, test before building:

1. Run 10 buyer interviews and 3 survey-expert interviews with a $15k single-study proposal.
2. Spend about $5k buying a small sample from 4-6 suppliers plus a Verasight control, and publish a free "state of sample quality" benchmark. This is the cheapest credibility asset, and the earlier file's idea is sound here.
3. Target the wedge of pollsters, publishers and litigation or pharma access studies, at $10-50k per study.
4. Partner for the control sample instead of recruiting, and use existing detection signals.
5. Consider co-opting or partnering with Signals & Standards before competing.

## 11. Gaps

- Funding for Verasight, Roundtable, dtect and CloudResearch was not found.
- Bot Olympics results are not yet published.
- There is no sourced count of enterprise sample buyers or typical corporate sample spend.
- There is no published per-recruit ABS cost.
- There is no litigation precedent on bot contamination.
- DQC and Signals & Standards pricing is unknown.
- The Verasight "independent validation" and Prolific "100% accuracy" claims are vendor-run.

# I0109-M3 Dossier: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds

Research date: 2026-10-13. Labels used below: FINDING (sourced), INFERENCE (my reasoning), GAP (not found).

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: do not advance as written. At best a small niche service; the venture-scale exchange is unproven and partly pre-empted.**

The prior competitor check marked this idea "gap" because its search budget was exhausted. That conclusion is wrong. Lender-side tools for the same job (payoff, repossession, charge-off refunds) already exist, are funded, and are growing:

- **F&I Sentinel**, PE-backed, with deep integration into the two big contracting platforms.
- **Lender Compliance Technologies (LCT)**, which launched a CUSO for credit unions on Sept 9, 2026, a month ago.
- **Allied Solutions RefundPlus**, a credit-union-focused product that explicitly covers charge-off.

The legal demand driver is real: regulators and state AGs do punish lenders for missed refunds. The remaining open space is narrow: pure contingency pricing, a charge-off focus, and an administrator-paid exchange. Nobody has shown administrators or carriers will pay.

## 2. Industry metrics (Step 0)

Operators here benchmark on:

- cancellations processed per year
- provider and administrator connections
- lenders served
- refund cycle time (the CFPB cited an 84-day average)
- cash recovered per eligible event
- regulator findings per exam

## 3. Market context and bottom-up sizing

**FINDINGS**

- Credit unions held $485.4B of auto loans at 2026Q2. There were 4,214 credit unions. 748 had assets over $500M. The 90th percentile asset size was $1.136B and the 75th was $281M. The system auto delinquency rate was 81 bps. ([NCUA Q2 2026](https://ncua.gov/files/publications/analysis/quarterly-data-summary-2026-Q2.pdf))
- Credit union used-auto charge-offs hit 1.11% over 12 months to March 2025, a record. ([CU Times on NCUA remarks](https://cutimes.com/2025/07/16/ncua-chair-kyle-hauptman-warns-of-rising-credit-risks)) Auto balances are flat to down, falling from 34% of credit union loans in 2019 to 28% in 2025. ([CU Times](https://www.cutimes.com/amp/2026/03/23/the-case-of-the-vanishing-credit-union-auto-loans/))
- US repossessions were 1.73M in 2024, the most since 2009 ([CNN via KTVZ](https://ktvz.com/money/cnn-business-consumer/2026/02/05/elizabeth-warren-launches-probe-into-booming-car-repossessions/)). Cox forecast about 1.8M for 2025 ([CURepossession](https://curepossession.com/how-many-cars-will-be-repossessed-in-2025/)). Fitch's subprime 60+ delinquency index set a record of 6.90% in January 2026 ([Auto Remarketing](https://www.autoremarketing.com/?p=107747)).
- The idea's "roughly 3M repossessions a year" is not supported. The higher figures come from repossession-assignment counts, which measure something different from repossessions ([CURepossession](https://curepossession.com/?p=34676)). Use about 1.7 to 1.8M.
- Add-on incidence at dealers: service contract penetration 44% and GAP 38% in Q3 2025, new and used combined ([StoneEagle via AutoSuccess](https://www.autosuccessonline.com/?p=68599)). No credit-union-indirect-specific rate was found.
- Allied reports an average GAP refund of $380, driven mostly by early payoffs ([Allied, Feb 2025](https://www.alliedsolutions.net/resources/allied-insights/the-gap-trap-blind-spots-that-could-cost-lenders-big)). Colorado credit union settlements imply GAP-only refunds of about $165 to $310 each, mostly payoffs: Ent $5.16M over 19,011 consumers ([CFM](https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2022/03/21/colorado-attorney-general-enters-into-settlements-with-credit-unions-requiring-refunds-of-gap-fees/)), Red Rocks $312K over 1,328 ([Law Week Colorado](https://www.lawweekcolorado.com/?p=81522)).

**INFERENCES**

- *Reachable customers.* A credit union with at least $200M of auto loans is roughly a $1B-asset institution at the system-average mix (auto is about 19% of assets: $485B of $2.5T). That implies roughly 400 to 450 credit unions, with a plausible range of 300 to 600 depending on auto concentration. Credit unions above about $5B (WSECU, for example) already buy from vendors. I could not count community banks.
- *Per-customer spend.* The idea's own model yields $40K to $47K a year per $1B-auto lender. At 450 lenders that is about $19M a year at 100% penetration. At a realistic 5 to 10% penetration after three years it is about $1M to $2M a year.
- *Cross-check from event counts.* Take 300K to 500K credit union auto charge-off events a year (my estimate). Apply 45% with add-ons, $700 unearned, and 60% unclaimed. That gives about $57M to $95M of unclaimed refunds and a fee pool of about $13M to $21M at 22.5%. The two methods converge on roughly $15M to $20M a year. That is a small company, not a venture outcome, unless Stages 2 and 3 work.
- *The $700 and 60% inputs are unverified.* Observed refunds run lower: $165 to $310 for GAP alone, and $380 average in Allied's data. The "60% unclaimed" figure has no source.

## 4. Competitors (Steps 4, 6, 7)

| Player | Evidence | Overlap |
|---|---|---|
| **F&I Sentinel** (Tallahassee; Calera Capital majority recap, March 2022) | Acquired Express Recoveries from Cox in Feb 2024 ([release](https://staging1.fandisentinel.com/?p=18844); [CB Insights](https://www.cbinsights.com/company/fi-sentinel/financials)). Integrated into Dealertrack and RouteOne, Jan 21, 2026 ([Auto Remarketing](https://www.autoremarketing.com/subprime/dealertrack-routeone-integrate-with-fi-sentinel-to-streamline-compliance-validation/)). Claims 1.75M cancellations a year, 150+ lenders and 600+ administrators (Inc. 5000 for the fourth year, Aug 2026; aggregator, not the company release: [BriefGlance](https://briefglance.com/articles/the-compliance-engine-how-one-firms-growth-signals-a-sea-change-in-auto-finance)). FAIRRCalc is a real-time refund-quote engine over a 190,000-form repository ([sheet](https://fandisentinel.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/FAIRRCalc-Solution-Sheet.pdf)). Sells "Look Backs" audits ([post](https://fandisentinel.com/?p=16600)). | **High.** It is already the closest thing to a neutral lender-to-administrator hub. |
| **LCT** (Dallas, founded 2021) | Refund Control: 1M+ cancellations, 100K+ a month capacity ([Jan 2026](https://www.autoremarketing.com/subprime/lender-compliance-technologies-passes-1-million-processed-vpp-cancellations/)). LCT CUSO launched Sept 9, 2026 with One Washington Financial (WSECU's CUSO), AKUVO's CEO and SWBC. Nearly 30 credit unions, 5M+ members ([Auto Remarketing](https://www.autoremarketing.com/?p=131056)). Aligns with the new GAPA/SCIC/MVPPA quote-portal standards ([Nov 2025](https://www.autoremarketing.com/subprime/lcts-refund-control-now-aligns-with-new-industry-standards-set-by-3-associations/)). | **High.** It has the idea's CUSO-distribution model already running. |
| **Allied Solutions RefundPlus** | Covers early payoff, repossession, total loss, charge-off and abandonment, plus a refund lockbox. Credit unions are the main customer base; 2022 NAFCU Innovation Award ([page](https://www.alliedsolutions.net/solutions/refund-plus)). | **High** on charge-off. |
| Dealertrack and RouteOne | Distribution layers, now partnered with F&I Sentinel. | Gatekeepers |
| Origence | No refund product found. | Partner or channel |
| In-house teams | A "back-end refund specialist" job posting surfaced in search but had expired when I opened it. | Existing workaround |

**Flags**

- Vendor figures conflict. LCT cites 600+, 800+ and 900+ provider connections on different pages, and workload reductions of 80%, 90% and 95%. F&I Sentinel's own site says 99+ lenders against 150+ in the August 2026 summary. Treat all as marketing.
- **No competitor discloses pricing.** I found no evidence that anyone offers contingency-only recovery. That is the idea's one clear Stage 1 differentiator, and it is unproven rather than confirmed absent.

**Moat view**

- Switching costs are moderate (workflow plus audit trail).
- Provider connections are the key scale asset, and incumbents have 4+ years of lead.
- Their network effects are same-side, not cross-side.

## 5. Demand and willingness to pay

**FINDINGS (hard)**

- CFPB Spring 2022: failing to request unearned GAP refunds from administrators and apply them after repossession is unfair. Refund errors inflated deficiency balances by hundreds of dollars ([CFPB blog](https://consumerfinance.gov/about-us/blog/overcharging-for-add-on-products-on-auto-loans); [Hudson Cook](https://hudsoncook.com/article/refunds-of-gap-and-other-voluntary-protection-products-a-federal-udaap-issue/)). Fall 2024: servicers "failed to refund" unused add-ons after early termination ([NIADA](https://niada.com/dashboard/cfpb-releases-supervisory-highlights-on-auto-finance/)).
- Colorado AG GAP actions: Wells Fargo $9.58M in Colorado and $82.4M multistate ([Law Week](https://www.lawweekcolorado.com/?p=66621)). Credit union settlements: Ent, Premier Members, Credit Union of Denver, Westerra ($846K over 3,422; [Colorado AG](https://coag.gov/press-releases/10-27-21)), Red Rocks, and Bellco and Canvas ($4M plus $100K penalty each) ([Consumer Finance Monitor](https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2023/01/11/credit-unions-settle-gap-fee-refund-cases-with-colorado-attorney-general/)).
- Liability is retroactive: Red Rocks covered Oct 2014 to Jul 2020, and Wells Fargo 2008 to 2018.
- Massachusetts consent orders in Nov 2024 required IronHorse to refund unearned GAP after repossession, with a $50K penalty ([Goodwin](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/blogs/2024/12/massachusetts-division-of-banks-issues-consent-orders-over-vehicle-repossession-practices)).
- Vendors have real traction (section 4). A funded, growing vendor set is itself evidence of paid demand.

**INFERENCES**

- Demand is **compliance-driven fear**, not "found money." Credit union buyers purchase audit-readiness. This confirms the earlier sharper-angle note that the pitch is liability reduction.
- The "small lenders rarely chase it" claim has no direct evidence. Colorado shows credit unions failed on payoffs. For repossession and charge-off the evidence is the CFPB findings.

**GAPS**

- Actual claim rates on repossession and charge-off refunds.
- Forum complaints and RFPs. Search returned no Reddit threads or RFPs.
- Competitor pricing.
- The "dealer chargeback stalling" claim is unverified.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

**FINDINGS**

- State law is a patchwork.
  - New Jersey, P.L. 2019 c.181: refund within 60 days of termination, "without requiring the borrower to request." The creditor may apply it to reduce the amount owed, and it may be paid to the creditor or administrator. The statute does not mention notifying the administrator ([NJ text](https://pub.njleg.gov/Bills/2018/PL19/181_.HTM)).
  - Alabama is similar.
  - Texas §354.007 lets the holder refund within 60 days or send instructions to the administrator within 30 days ([Texas](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._fin._code_section_354.007)).
  - Colorado §5-9.3-106, effective Jan 1, 2024, covers repossession and sets assignee and administrator reimbursement mechanics ([statute](https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_5-9.3-106)).
  - California AB 2311, effective Jan 2023 ([F&I Sentinel](https://staging1.fandisentinel.com/?p=16110)).
- **The informational thesis is validated.** The creditor is often the only party who knows the loan ended, and administrators and dealers "won't initiate the cancellation" without notice ([Allied state compilation, Sept 2020](https://lists.simplelists.com/cu_fly-in_attorneys/cache/21034478/2.pdf/)). The market response so far has been lender-side tools, because regulators put the burden on creditors.
- **Federal retreat is real.** The CFPB brought one auto enforcement action in 2025, terminated the Toyota Motor Credit consent order in May 2025, and proposed raising the larger-participant threshold ([Goodwin](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/03/insights-finance-cfs-yir-auto-loan-origination-and-servicing)). A GAO-based report puts staff down about 88% (secondary: [GetOutOfDebt](https://getoutofdebt.org/242299/cfpb-downsizing-gao-report-consumer-impact)). State AGs are active: 41 AGs settled with Credit Acceptance on Sept 17, 2026 for about $710M ([Jenner](https://www.jenner.com/en/news-insights/client-alerts/regulation-in-the-midst-of-deregulation-state-ags-fill-the-federal-enforcement-void)).

**INFERENCES (need counsel)**

- *Who owns the money.* The refund legally belongs to the consumer and must be credited to the deficiency (Hudson Cook, above). It is not simply "the lender's own cash." The lender's gain is a smaller write-off. When the refund exceeds the deficiency, or no deficiency exists, the lender gets nothing.
- *The fee.* A contingency fee has to be paid from the lender's funds. Wisconsin guidance bars deducting processing fees from the customer's refund ([Wisconsin DFI](https://dfi.wi.gov/Pages/FinancialServices/LicensedFinancial/GAPComplianceInformationForDealers.aspx)).
- *The free retrospective audit.* It creates a written record of past noncompliance and invites UDAAP exposure. That is a sales obstacle and a legal-privilege problem for the vendor.
- *Pooled cross-lender data.* It raises Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) consumer-reporting-agency questions if the data is used for eligibility decisions. De-identified actuarial use is lower risk. See [NCLC](https://library.nclc.org/article/data-gatherers-evading-fcra-may-find-themselves-still-hot-water). The Gramm-Leach-Bliley (GLBA) service-provider exception does not settle FCRA status.

## 7. Stage 2 and 3: the exchange

- *Administrators paying $2 to $5 per attested event.* GAPA, SCIC and MVPPA published minimum standards for refund-quote portals in late 2025, aimed at vendors, with administrator and lender input ([SCIC](https://go-scic.com/2025/10/scic-publishes-new-minimum-standards-to-drive-efficiencies/)). The industry is standardizing through trade associations and incumbent vendors. F&I Sentinel already links 600+ administrators. I found **no evidence that administrators pay for lender-attested intake**.
- *Carriers and reinsurers paying $50K to $250K for termination curves.* No analog found. StoneEagle's public benchmark reports cover dealer F&I profit and penetration, not cancellation curves ([StoneEagle](https://www.se-fi.com/post/stoneeagledata-record-breaking-f-i-performance-in-q1)). Dealer-owned reinsurer float economics were not documented in reliable sources.
- *Incentive problem.* Whoever holds unearned premium gains from slow refunds. That makes administrators and dealer reinsurers payers with mixed incentives. This inference is unverified.
- *Open-schema strategy.* An open schema competes with association standards and vendor APIs that already exist.

## 8. Why-now check

- **Real:** record subprime stress, repossessions at 2009-era highs, state AGs and private plaintiffs filling the federal gap, and the California CARS Act (effective Oct 2026) and the NY FAIR Act as signs of tightening state action ([Goodwin](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/03/insights-finance-cfs-yir-auto-loan-origination-and-servicing)). Sen. Warren opened a voluntary inquiry into repossessions at 12 lenders in Feb 2026 ([CNN via KTVZ](https://ktvz.com/money/cnn-business-consumer/2026/02/05/elizabeth-warren-launches-probe-into-booming-car-repossessions/)).
- **Weak for this segment:** credit union delinquency is 0.81% versus about 6.9% in subprime ABS. Most repossession growth sits at finance companies, not credit unions.
- **Unverified:** the LLM cost claim ("cents per case"). Incumbents already hold form repositories and automation.
- **Net:** the why-now supports the category. It does not support a new entrant's edge over vendors launched in 2021 to 2024.

## 9. Synthesis

**Durable advantages of the idea**

- Contingency pricing removes budget friction, if the lender accepts it.
- A charge-off and repossession specialism could beat generalist payoff-first tools.

**Structural vulnerabilities**

- Three funded incumbents already sell the same core function to credit unions.
- LCT's CUSO covers the idea's cooperative-distribution plan.
- Stage 2 and 3 payers are unproven.
- The refund legally belongs to the consumer.
- The fee pool for the credit union segment is roughly $15M to $20M a year.

**Trajectory:** incumbents are consolidating distribution (Dealertrack, RouteOne, CUSOs, associations).

| Scenario | Probability | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Bull: exchange adopted | 5% | An incumbent or association partners with it |
| Base: small contingency service, $0.5M to $2M a year | 35% | Niche credit union and agency channel |
| Bear: no traction or acqui-hire | 60% | Incumbents bundle charge-off recovery; sales cycles stall |

## 10. Cheapest tests before any build

1. Ask LCT, F&I Sentinel and Allied for pricing and whether they offer success-fee or charge-off recovery.
2. Interview 10 credit union collections managers for the current repossession refund workflow and claim rate.
3. Ask three GAP administrators whether they would pay for structured loan-end notices.
4. Get a short opinion from counsel on contingency fee, deficiency offset, and the audit-privilege structure.

## 11. Unresolved items

- No competitor pricing.
- No claim-rate data.
- No community-bank count.
- No cross-lender event data.
- The California SB 766 cite in the parent idea remains unverified; I did not recheck it.

# I0428-M1 Dossier: Line-Keyed Cross-Examination Kits for LOP Defense

Research date: 2026-10-13. About 45 searches and fetches. Claims marked [unverified] rest on one secondary source or on my inference.

## Verdict

Re-scope; do not build as written. The idea has real forced-spend triggers and a plausible product. But the "gap" finding does not survive checking in Texas, because a Texas counteraffidavit industry already sells the signed-coder layer. The testimony profit center faces documented exclusion risk in Georgia's federal courts. No source confirms the $395 price point, the $3-5k expert-cost premise or the carrier pre-approval threshold. The surviving core is the line-keyed cross-examination package plus provider-bias work-up, which I found no one selling. Best entry: Georgia or Texas, sold as a counteraffidavit-plus-cross bundle, after mystery-shopping incumbents for price.

## 1. Market context (bottom-up)

**Claims backdrop.** Auto bodily injury payouts passed physical damage for the first time: BI was 52.3% of combined BI and PD dollars, up from 44.4% in 2022. Average third-party medical expenses submitted rose to $32,300 in Q1 2026 from $24,300 in Q1 2023 (CCC data, [Claims Journal, Aug 2026](https://amp.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2026/08/06/339296.htm)). This supports "medical specials are rising and contested." It is not LOP-specific.

**Volume.** Texas courts saw 61,782 motor-vehicle injury/damage civil filings in FY2024, up 16% ([OCA FY2024 highlights](https://txcourts.gov/media/1459785/2024-ar-highlights.pdf)). The extracted text does not state the court levels covered. I found no Georgia equivalent and no LOP-prevalence statistic for any wedge state. The only prevalence datapoint is an unverified Publix lawyer's claim that about two-thirds of its Florida slip-and-fall claims involve LOPs ([KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/republish/courts/letters-of-protection-personal-injury-cases-surprise-bills/)).

**Reachable buyers.** No count of 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques exists in public sources. Proxies from press releases surfaced in search (2010-2019, stale, pages not individually fetched): the Texas Association of Defense Counsel cited 1,500+ members in 2019 and up to 2,000 earlier; the Georgia Defense Lawyers Association cited about 920. My estimate: 80-150 wedge firms across Houston and Atlanta, once large panel firms and carrier staff counsel are excluded [inference].

**Revenue ceiling.** The finalist's own mix is 12 firms x 5 kits x $395, about $23.7k/month. With 10-15% upsell to $1,900 declarations, that adds $11-17k/month. At 100 firms and the same mix, the metro-wedge SAM is roughly $3-5M/year [inference]. This is a good lifestyle business or a seed-stage wedge, not a venture-scale market by itself.

**What I did not find:** any vendor selling a bill-line-keyed cross-examination outline, a provider-bias sheet, or a factor-price comparison. Defense commentary already tells lawyers to probe referral percentages, testimony frequency, lien dependence and charge-master practices ([ALFA International](https://www.alfainternational.com/publications_news/dont-let-inflated-medical-billing-and-provider-bias-take-the-wind-out-of-your-sails/)). That means the know-how is public. The product is packaging plus a signature.

## 3. Incumbents who could add this

- **Enlyte/CCC:** distribution to carriers is strong, but both sell to adjusters. Testimony and counsel-facing work product conflict with that channel. Likelier move: partner or refer.
- **Texas counteraffidavit shops:** most likely to copy. They already hold coder networks and defense relationships; adding an LLM-drafted cross outline is a template exercise [inference].
- **General legal-AI tools:** a defense associate can ask a generalist LLM to turn an itemized bill into cross questions. The unique value is the credentialed signature and defensible benchmark data, not the outline [inference].

## 4. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Forced spend (strongest evidence):**
- *Texas § 18.001.* A counteraffidavit must be served by the earliest of 120 days after the defendant's answer or the expert-designation deadline; it must be sworn and give reasonable notice of its basis ([statute text](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._civ._practice_and_remedies_code_section_18.001), last amended 2019). The Texas Supreme Court upheld a nurse-CPC counteraffidavit and declined full Daubert gatekeeping at that stage ([*In re Allstate*, 2021](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1452189/200071.pdf); [summary](https://www.mdjwlaw.com/newsroom/news/TIN-20210510-Item2)). *Ortiz v. Nelapatla* (reported May 2026) held affidavits are assessed item by item, so partial challenges leave unchallenged charges admissible ([SMU](https://www.smu.edu/law/news-events/2026/advocacy-team-wins-texas-supreme-court-decision)). Line-by-line audit output is therefore well matched to Texas practice.
- *Georgia SB 68 (signed April 21, 2025).* Juries may see billed and paid amounts; LOP-related information is discoverable per secondary summaries, including referral source and sale of receivables ([Jones Day](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2025/04/georgia-enacts-major-tort-reform-legislation); [DLA Piper](https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2025/05/georgia-enacts-sweeping-tort-reform)). The medical-expense provisions apply only to causes of action arising on or after April 21, 2025 (Jones Day). With a two-year limitations period, the volume of qualifying suits builds through 2027 [inference].
- *Florida § 768.0427* already mandates disclosure of the LOP, coded itemized bills and factoring purchase price ([statute](https://florida.public.law/statutes/fla._stat._768.0427)); appellate guidance on it is thin ([Sept/Oct 2025 article](https://mydigitalpublication.com/article/Evidence+/5039476/852249/article.html)).

**Carrier spend on adjacent services:** Enlyte markets "$5-7K improvement in average settlement" and up to $30,000 LAE savings per 100 demands (vendor claims, same Enlyte page). That implies carrier willingness to pay in the low hundreds of dollars per package [inference].

**Not found:** forum complaints, RFPs, published counteraffidavit prices, or any quote validating $395 or "$3-5k". General expert benchmarks are $356/hr for review, $448/hr for deposition and $478/hr for trial ([Expert Institute](https://www.theexpertinstitute.com/expert-witness-fees)). At those rates $3,500/day testimony is market, and $3-5k is plausible for a report plus testimony but is not documented.

**Efficacy caveat:** a plaintiff-side Georgia firm argues jurors rarely debate fair price once a procedure is deemed necessary ([Kastorf](https://kastorflaw.com/analysis/medical-billing-experts/)). A Louisiana note finds billing experts cannot reduce awards there at all ([LSU Law Review](https://lawreview.law.lsu.edu/?p=2981)). Willingness to pay depends on outcomes that I could not measure.

## 5. Unit economics

- Kit: $395 price, $40-90 marginal cost (founder estimate, unverified), implying 77-90% gross margin. Coder wage was not researched.
- Real costs are outside the estimate: retained testifying coders, Daubert defense, E&O insurance, data-licensing (Context4 versus TiC engineering) and sales to a fragmented buyer.
- Upsell math: the finalist's 10-15% attach rate fits Texas, where a counteraffidavit is a near-mandatory early step. In Georgia I verified no equivalent affidavit regime, so attach rate there is likely lower [inference].
- Panel-counsel hourly rates (the ROI comparison) could not be found; carrier guidelines are private.

## 6. Regulatory, liability and admissibility

- **Texas:** coders qualify for counteraffidavits (*Allstate*), so the signature is a commodity there; trial testimony still faces ordinary Rule 702 scrutiny [inference from the stage-limited holding].
- **Georgia/11th Circuit:** *Young v. Panera* (M.D. Fla. Aug 2024) excluded a defense coding expert who relied on national averages, finding no expertise on reasonableness and unfair prejudice that outweighed value; it cites *Frushtick v. FeroExpress* (N.D. Ga. 2022) and others ([case page](https://www.flexlaw.co/case/1419574/2024-young-v-panera-llc), AI-generated summary; verify the opinion). Other courts admitted a Context4-based coder (*Cordero v. Target*, [Marshall Dennehey](https://www.marshalldennehey.com/thought-leadership/overcoming-the-daubert-challenge-with-your-billing-and-coding-expert)). Exclusion risk is real, and it directly undermines "testimony is the profit center."
- **New benchmark risk:** no court decision found accepting Transparency-in-Coverage rates as reasonable-value proof. The Allstate-approved method is a UCR database.
- **Bias attack on the vendor:** "kits as funnel, testimony as margin" invites cross on the coder's financial interest in repeat defense work, the same attack the kit teaches [inference]. Separating the kit author from the testifying expert, and keeping consulting work product privileged, needs counsel review (no source found).
- **UPL, E&O and AI-error liability:** not researched; a gap.
- **Statutes not enacted:** Texas SB 30 (LOP disclosure, paid-amount limit) died in conference May 2025 ([LegiScan summary](https://legiscan.com/TX/bill/SB30)). HB 2446 (affidavit alone sufficient up to $50,000) passed the House engrossed; final status unverified ([text](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/HB02446E.htm)). If enacted, it would weaken the Texas counteraffidavit market's role in small files.

## 7. Is the why-now real?

- **Real:** Georgia SB 68 (post-April 2025 claims), record BI severity, and scaled plaintiff AI. Plaintiff AI raises demand volume but no source ties it to defense expert spend.
- **Misframed:** Texas had no new LOP statute (SB 30 failed). Its counteraffidavit workflow dates from 2019-2021.
- **Premature/thin:** The 2026 TiC final rule (published Oct 6, 2026) removes implausible provider-service rates, adds taxonomy and utilization files, and lowers the allowed-amount claim threshold from 20 to 11. Rate-file changes apply 5 months after publication; the new contextual files, 11 months ([CMS fact sheet](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/transparency-coverage-final-rules-cms-9882-f); [Turquoise analysis](https://turquoise.health/resources/blog/transparency-in-coverage-final-rule-2026-what-changes-for-payer-machine-readable-files)). The "same billing TIN's own negotiated rates" anchor only exists where the LOP provider is in a payer network. LOP care often bypasses health insurance ([TMLT](https://www.tmlt.org/risk-alerts/what-physicians-should-know-about-letters-of-protection); [KFF](https://kffhealthnews.org/republish/courts/letters-of-protection-personal-injury-cases-surprise-bills/)). Expect many blank anchors [inference].
- The factor-price anchor is statutory only in Florida; in Texas and Georgia it depends on discovery success.

## 8. Moat assessment

- Track-record asset (Daubert/cross survival): potentially strong, but slow to build and fragile if one ruling goes wrong.
- Switching costs: weak; kits are per-file.
- Data: weak; Medicare, TiC and Context4 are all available to rivals.
- Process power (LLM pre-code plus coder sign-off): moderate, quickly copied.

## 9. Validation steps (cheap, in order)

1. Mystery-shop MedCost Contain, IMS Legal, No World Borders and Health Law Network for counteraffidavit and testimony quotes. If a Texas counteraffidavit costs under about $500, the kit's price edge disappears.
2. Run the 15 defense-lawyer calls to confirm the pre-approval threshold; a desk search found none (old ethics opinions say pre-approval interferes with counsel's judgment, [RI 1999](https://ezel.ai/ethics-opinions/rieap/99-18-insurer-litigation-guidelines-and-independent-judgment)).
3. Pull 20 real LOP bills and test how many providers appear in any payer's TiC files. Under about 40% coverage, redesign the benchmark around Context4/UCR plus Medicare.
4. Ask for one Georgia state-court ruling admitting a coder on reasonable value. If none exists, drop the testimony thesis.

## Remaining gaps

LOP prevalence, defense-boutique counts, expert fee data, panel hourly rates, HB 2446 status and Georgia statute text (secondary sources only).

# I0715-M1 Dossier: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates

Saved at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-asherperemel/2d21b2bf-d792-4998-b326-860505fc728f/scratchpad/biz/deep/I0715-M1_dossier.md`.

Research date: 2026-10-13. Basis: roughly 45 searches and fetches, including the CDI task force report and the April 2026 Assembly committee analysis, both text-searched in full.

## Verdict

**Conditional and weaker than the pitch.** The pain is real and documented, but the stated why-now is partly wrong. AB 1795 appears not to reach the Eaton and Palisades claims the wedge targets. The insurer's 30-day inspection is elective, not a duty. A free, NSF-funded AI report-reader is already in development, and a funded PA-software startup (Finch) sits in the buyer's inbox. Realistic year-one revenue is about $0.1M-$0.5M, not $1.5M-$2.5M (my estimate, derived in section 4).

If it proceeds, it should be reframed as workflow software for policyholder-side CIHs, litigators and PAs, built on existing claims-handling law. It should not be sold as an "AB 1795 letter generator" for the January 2025 fires.

## 1. Why-now audit: what holds and what does not

**Holds**
- AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a rebuttable smoke-source presumption and makes insurers pay for "necessary" sampling and testing ([CDI release](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0102-alerts/2026/upload/091526-Consumer-Alert-California-protects-families-from-hidden-smoke-damage-after-wildfires.pdf)).
- The dispute is real. CDI's task force says more than 40,000 claims were filed, more than 13,000 of them standing homes with smoke damage. It cites conflicting views on how and where to sample, no uniform standards, and allegations of biased experts ([CDI task force report](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/140-catastrophes/upload/CDI-Smoke-Claims-and-Remediation-Task-Force-Report-030926.pdf)).
- The litigation wave is real:
  - Ghazarian v. Fire Insurance Exchange and HygieneTech, a proposed class action ([Singleton Schreiber](https://www.singletonschreiber.com/newsroom/pressreleases/Lawsuit-Filed-Against-Farmers-Insurance-for-Bad-Faith-Smoke-Damage-Practices)), plus a second class action against hygiene vendors ([Recorder via firm](https://www.singletonschreiber.com/newsroom/news/hygiene-companies-face-class-actions-over-alleged-failure-to-properly-test-homes-for-toxins-after-eaton-wildfire)).
  - A federal suit against State Farm and its vendor EFI Global ([firm release](https://singleton.sitepilot11.firmseek.com/newsroom/pressreleases/lawsuit-filed-against-state-farm-and-environmental-consultant-for-bad-faith-smoke-damage-practices)).
  - LA County v. State Farm, 8/31/2026 ([Spectrum](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/ca/california/wildfires/2026/08/31/la-county-state-farm-lawsuit-wildfire-claims)).
  - A county probe of Farmers ([Insurance Business](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/catastrophe/la-county-opens-investigation-into-farmers-over-wildfire-claims-handling-589622.aspx)).
  - Beutner v. Chubb, filed October 2026 ([Hoodline](https://hoodline.com/2026/10/ex-lausd-chief-austin-beutner-sues-chubb-over-toxic-palisades-home/)).

**Does not hold, or is overstated**
- **No retroactivity.** Hoodline states that neither AB 1642 nor AB 1795 "applies retroactively" ([Hoodline](https://hoodline.com/2026/10/ex-lausd-chief-austin-beutner-sues-chubb-over-toxic-palisades-home/)). Merlin Law Group analyses say the principal testing, payment and restoration provisions apply prospectively to residential claims on or after the operative date ([Merlin 9/30/2026](https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/blog/california-wildfire-smoke-laws/); [Merlin follow-up](https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/?p=46909)). The April 2026 committee analysis applied provisions to policies issued, amended or renewed on or after the operative date ([Assembly analysis](https://ains.assembly.ca.gov/media/364)). The "AB 1795 deficiency letter" therefore cannot be a statutory demand on January 2025 claims. At best it is a persuasive benchmark.
- **Inspection is elective.** Merlin says insurer inspection is optional, with the 30-day clock applying only if the insurer elects to inspect. The CalMatters digest says insurers that choose to inspect must do so within 30 days ([digest](https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1795)). The pitch's "30-day inspection duty" is wrong.
- **Testing is not automatic.** Kennedys' Brandon Sipple notes the law does not require professional testing of every impact-zone home and does not "dispense with" proving smoke damage is present ([Claims Journal](https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2026/10/08/340579.htm)).
- **No statutory adequacy yardstick.** Merlin's analysis does not say who is qualified to test or what a sampling plan must contain, and I found no source saying the statute defines either. DTSC lead and asbestos standards are due end-2028, other contaminants end-2029 ([CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/09/new-law-smoke-damage-in-homes/)). The Grid would be self-authored, not statutory.
- **The "inadequate sampling" premise is contested science.**
  - AIHA guide authors told the task force that smoke, ash and soot are accepted surrogates, that targeted sampling against background is correct, and that "exhaustive sampling" is unnecessary ([CDI report, summary and Section III.B](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/140-catastrophes/upload/CDI-Smoke-Claims-and-Remediation-Task-Force-Report-030926.pdf)).
  - A scorecard citing AIHA to penalize low sample counts invites a rebuttal that quotes AIHA.
  - Comparing results to background, which the pitch treats as a flaw, is the AIHA-endorsed method.
- **A closing litigation window.** Suits on the 2025 fires are generally due by 1/7/2027 under Ins. Code 2071's 24-month period, though tolling is argued ([Hoodline](https://hoodline.com/2026/10/ex-lausd-chief-austin-beutner-sues-chubb-over-toxic-palisades-home/); [A&A Law](https://aa.law/blog/eaton-fire-claim-deadline-2026/)). Demand for report triage may spike before that date. Building and validating by then is a stretch.

## 2. Demand and willingness-to-pay evidence

- A United Policyholders survey (n=453 households, about 154 standing homes, self-selected) found 52% of standing-home respondents said the insurer "brought in experts they didn't trust," and only 3% reported no claim problems. It also found 83% of standing-home respondents had hired professional help (type undefined) and 86% had not moved back ([UP report](https://uphelp.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/REPORT_-2025-LA-Wildfires-6-Month-Survey-Results.pdf)).
- Current spend on workarounds:
  - Independent hygienist testing runs $2,000-$20,000+ ([Kerley Schaffer](https://www.kerleyschaffer.com/blog/fair-plan-hygenist-testing-guide)).
  - One family paid about $17,000 and another about $10,000. A consultant offered seven samples for $3,500, and an insurer paid one vendor $25,000 for a single inspection ([Consumer Watchdog transcript](https://consumerwatchdog.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Smoke-Mirrors-Episode-2-The-Underworld-of-Fire-Insurance-Subcontractors.txt)).
- A policyholder-side attorney reports that insurer hygienists took no more than ten samples in a 3,000 sq ft home and skipped wall cavities, attic insulation and HVAC unless the insured paid ([Merlin, 2025](https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/blog/california-wildfire-smoke-claims/)). This is an advocate's account. The Consumer Watchdog transcript independently describes six tape lifts and a 15-sample job.
- PA fees run roughly 5%-15% of settlement ([UP](https://uphelp.org/what-southern-california-wildfire-victims-can-expect-from-their-insurance-adjuster/)). A $395 audit is small against that if it moves outcomes.
- **Not found:** any evidence that a deficiency letter changes carrier behavior. I also found no PA, attorney or carrier purchase, RFP or pilot for report-adequacy scoring. The $40k-$150k plaintiff analytics price is unvalidated.

## 3. Competitive landscape

|---|---|---|---|
| **Purdue / Tufts / UCLA FIRE-WUI project** | Plans an "AI-supported platform that translates home environmental testing reports into understandable summaries with contextual comparisons," to be "publicly available." Holds 500+ submitted reports and shares results with CDI ([Purdue deck](https://engineering.purdue.edu/PlumbingSafety/resources/Palisades-Community-Council-May-2026.pdf); [Tufts](https://sites.google.com/tufts.edu/nsf-fire-recovery-study/)) | NSF grants of about $1.32M total, running to Jan 2029 ([Palipost](https://palipost.com/?p=112189)) | **High.** Same ingestion step, free, credible, and has a bigger dataset than the 25 reports in the 30-day plan. Explanatory, not adversarial. No launch date. |
| **Finch** | "Full-claim intelligence platform" for public adjusters. Reports 315,000 documents across 15,000+ claims, and says PA estimates averaged about 50% above carrier in a sample ([Claims Journal](https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2026/09/29/340380.htm)) | $4.5M round, 9/29/2026 | **High as channel or acquirer.** It owns the PA inbox and could add an IH-report module. |
| **InsuranceClaim123** | $295 CarFax-style estimate review for homeowners, 3-5 day turnaround, launched Jan 2026 ([FinTech Global](https://fintech.global/2026/01/15/property-owners-get-new-way-to-verify-insurer-estimates/)) | Undisclosed | Medium. It sets the $295 consumer anchor and could extend to smoke. |

- **Incumbents.** I found no evidence that Verisk, CCC, Cotality, Sedgwick or Crawford sell IH-report analytics. Crawford says it has hygienists under contract ([Claims Journal](https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2026/10/08/340579.htm)). IICRC S760, a wildfire-smoke restoration standard, is still in development. Final standards could embed their own audit logic.

- **Adjacent analogs in legal AI.** Parambil (plaintiff medical-record review) listed a $6M seed in January 2026 ([listing](https://neuronfeed.com/startups/parambil)). Bloomberg Law covers AI in mass-tort intake ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/ai-is-disrupting-mass-torts-with-the-promise-of-lower-costs)). Plaintiff-side buyers do pay for AI triage.

## 4. Bottom-up market size

My estimates, with assumptions stated:

- **Reachable homes.** 13,000 standing-home smoke claims (CDI). If PAs represent 30%-50% of them (assumed, because I found no PA count), that is about 3,900-6,500 homes. If 30%-50% of those still have a disputed carrier IH report, that is about 1,200-3,250 homes.
- **PA audits.** At 10%-20% paid conversion in 12 months, that is 120-650 audits. At $395 that is **$47k-$257k**. Subscriptions add little, because PA tools price at $99-$250 a month ([ClaimWizard](https://claimwizard.com/pricing/)).
- **Plaintiff analytics.** At most 0-2 pilots in year one at $25k-$75k, or **$0-$150k**. Plaintiff-side activity is concentrated: Singleton Schreiber brought both class actions and the State Farm/EFI suit. Buyer concentration is therefore high, and none has been shown to buy.
- **Year-one total, about $0.1M-$0.5M.** The pitch's math puts 15% of 13,000 at about $770k, so its $1.5M-$2.5M depends on $0.7M-$1.7M of unvalidated analytics contracts. 100% penetration of 13,000 homes at $395 would be only $5.1M.
- **Lumpy and event-driven.** Post-2027 TAM depends on future declared-emergency wildfires reaching urban standing homes. Other states have no comparable statute; I found none.

## 5. Unit economics

- **Gross margin.** If human QA takes 1-1.5 hours at $60-$150 an hour, plus LLM and OCR costs, gross margin on a $395 audit is plausibly 55%-80%. This is an assumption.
- **The $900 CIH-signed plan** splits 50/50, leaving about $450 for CIH time at the quoted $150 an hour. That works only if review takes about three hours or less, and it carries liability (section 6).
- **Customer acquisition.** The channel is small and relational, with PAs reached through associations and attorneys through referrals. CAC should be low at the start, but the market is shallow (assumption, no CAC data found).
- **Data moat.** The "largest labeled dataset" claim is weak. Purdue already holds 500+ reports ([Purdue deck](https://engineering.purdue.edu/PlumbingSafety/resources/Palisades-Community-Council-May-2026.pdf)), and EFRU had mapped 81 homes by April 2025 ([report](https://www.click2houston.com/news/national/2025/04/11/in-fight-over-insurance-neighbors-crowdsource-la-fire-contamination-data/)). Pooling client reports also raises consent and work-product issues.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **CIH sign-off.** California does not license industrial hygienists generally. The CIH is a title-protected credential, and Cal/OSHA only requires "competent" supervision of exposure monitoring. A petition to define CIH as competent is pending ([Cal/OSHA staff evaluation](https://www.dir.ca.gov/oshsb/documents/petition-612-staffeval.pdf)). A non-CIH can therefore draft a plan, but credibility needs a CIH.
- **Certification risk.** The April bill version had CalEPA certify IHs, restorers and labs by 1/1/2028 and CDI certify adjusters and PAs ([Assembly analysis](https://ains.assembly.ca.gov/media/364)). The chaptered digest mentions only adjuster and PA training and Cal/OSHA worker certification ([digest](https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1795)). Which version survived is unverified.
- **PA licensing and direct-to-consumer exposure.** Ins. Code 15007 defines a public adjuster as anyone who, for compensation, "acts on behalf of or aids in any manner" an insured in negotiating a claim, and 15006 bars unlicensed activity ([CDI](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0200-industry/0050-renew-license/0200-requirements/public-adjuster/Authorizing-Act.cfm)). Selling a $295 statute-cited demand letter to homeowners could be argued to be unlicensed adjusting or unauthorized practice of law. I found no authority either way. Selling to licensed PAs and attorneys is safer.
- **Expert and liability exposure.** The scorecard is not an expert opinion. Expert-admissibility fights over qualifications and methodology are a general risk (not sourced in this research). An error that sinks a claim creates E&O exposure for the vendor and the CIH of record.
- **Referral fees.** A testing-firm referral fee on a tool sold to the policyholder side invites bias attacks, so zero fees is cleaner.

## 7. Risks, tests and sharper angle

- **Kill tests** (before building much):
  - Do 10 PAs or attorneys with live files pay $395 after a free audit?
  - Does any carrier reconsider after receiving a scorecard-based letter?
  - Will two policyholder-side CIHs say the Grid matches how they would attack a report?
  - Does the Purdue team confirm a launch date and whether its platform stays explanatory?
- **Sharper angle.**
  - Sell to the scarce policyholder-side CIHs and litigation experts as extraction-plus-gap-list workflow software. They testify, so the buyer-wants-a-testifying-expert objection disappears.
  - Use existing law as the hook: the carrier's duty to investigate and the CDI market-conduct findings. Use AB 1795 and AB 1642 as persuasive benchmarks.
  - Keep a version-controlled Grid so it re-maps to the 2028-29 DTSC standards and to future fires.
  - Pursue data-sharing with Purdue and EFRU rather than racing them.

## 8. Gaps and unverified items

- The chaptered AB 1795 text could not be read. leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returned a Cloudflare 403. Non-retroactivity rests on two secondary sources and the April analysis. The "qualified person" and "certification" points are unconfirmed.
- No count of licensed California PAs or of PA-represented smoke claims was found.
- The Purdue "free review" is documented only as one-on-one household meetings and the research platform. No formal SLA or capacity limit was confirmed.
- The sampling-density and skipped-zone claims come from advocates and are not independently verified.
- I found no data on how many Eaton and Palisades smoke claims are still open and disputed.

objections: The 'scarce verified-human control + recalibration' asset is not scarce, and the players who own it can add an audit line item faster than a startup can build credibility. SSRS already sells Encipher Nonprob, which calibrates opt-in samples bought from outside vendors against probability-panel benchmarks. It claims a >30% median selection-bias reduction (vendor-reported, and it targets selection bias, not fraud, so the overlap is partial). It also says hybrid designs with a parallel probability sample are preferred, which is the control-group design in this pitch. Verasight has a 200,000+ verified panel with Ivy-League and 100+ institutional customers. It already published a Pew-style benchmarking replication, so a 'neutral' audit is one product page away for it. Ipsos owns KnowledgePanel plus Xperiti/Vepp respondent verification. A verified control rents for $3.50-5 per complete or about $12.5k for n=1,000 on Ipsos omnibus, so the middleman only adds a stats template and a brand. Pre-mortem cause #1: Verasight, SSRS or Ipsos sells 'independent validation' using academic partners, and buyers accept it.

The neutrality niche is being claimed right now by better-credentialed entrants, and this industry has a proven way to co-opt referees: sellers pay them. Signals & Standards (John Bremer, ex-NPD/Circana and Toluna, on the Insights Association standards committee) launched Sept 2026 as 'independent by design'. It audits suppliers' quality claims on process and results and offers named personal validation. Data Quality Co-op, an independent clearinghouse with a 0-1000 Data Trust Score, is being embedded into Sago, Dig Insights and Advertiser Perceptions in 2026. 'Independent validation' therefore reaches end buyers bundled inside their agencies' platforms, with no separate audit purchase. Dynata paid for Neutronian's NQI certification. Suppliers pay CIRQ for ISO 20252 certification. Money flows seller to referee, so a buyer-funded per-study auditor has no precedent. Lucid's 2016 Fulcrum Quality ranking was run by the platform, and I found no evidence it persists. The competition pass called the neutral-auditor gap open, but the gap is closing from both the solo-veteran side and the DQC-plus-agency-distribution side.

Buyers' revealed response to this exact problem is not to hire a per-study auditor, and the audit costs more than what it protects. Procter & Gamble required ISO 20252 certification for online sample suppliers by July 2025, with annual surveillance audits, which pushes the audit onto sellers. The FT audits vendors itself. Prolific offers a '100% Human Guarantee' that refunds twice the response cost. After YouGov's failure, the Bible Society's remedy was to ask the vendor again. A Jaguar Land Rover insights director says clients want quality but will not pay the difference. Greenbook's 2020 piece says buyers blanch at about $3 per complete and a 10-cent price gap decides awards. A 1,000-complete study costs about $3-5k in sample, so a $3-15k audit is 1-4 times the fieldwork bill. The unit economics only clear at $10k or more per study (8-38% margin at $10k, loss at $3k). The real competitors are non-consumption, switching to a direct panel, and a vendor refund. This is a Jobs-to-be-Done failure, not a feature gap.

The detection and retrospective-audit half has no pricing power and is consolidating into bundles, so the startup would resell its competitors' signals. ReDem already batch-processes uploaded post-field CSV/Excel files and offers a Quality Report with an optional Quality Seal. Rep Data acquired ReDem in Feb 2026, keeps it as a standalone product and bundles it with Research Defender. DQC runs post-field supplier scorecards. Prolific ships free bot authenticity checks inside Qualtrics. Verisoul costs $99-350 a month. Cint ships its own Trust Score. The dossier's plan to 'ingest signals from dtect, DQC or Verisoul' and rent the control panel from Verasight, NORC or Ipsos makes the startup dependent on firms that are (a) each able to build the analytics layer and (b) able to cut off data or API access. Against Helmer's 7 Powers it has no cornered resource (the control is rentable), no scale or switching costs on day one, and its only reachable power is branding, which takes years. The remaining value is a signed report plus a method that SSRS, Pew and Verasight have already published.

The high-stakes wedges (litigation, pharma, pollsters/publishers) have incumbents or substitutes, and no buyer pull exists. Litigation: survey experts already bill about $15-20k all-in for a survey and could add a control themselves. I found no ruling excluding a survey for bots or fraudulent panelists, so no one has to buy an audit. Pharma: respondent-identity vendors already exist (Ipsos-owned Vepp, Assure BrandPanels), and EphMRA's work on this runs through members-only webinars, not a procured audit. Polling publishers: Pew and NORC publish the method free and run address-recruited panels, so the most credible possible customers are also the most credible competitors. An audit stamp invites professional-liability and trade-libel exposure that a solo or small team cannot absorb. Simile's $200M raise on synthetic respondents threatens to shrink the panel spend that defines the market. A serviceable market of about $10-25M (the dossier's own estimate) cannot fund a trust-brand build against these incumbents.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Any of the following would move this from serious toward manageable. (1) At least 3 of 10 insights heads or agency research directors sign a paid pilot at $10k or more for a single-study audit. Interest does not count; a signed purchase order or invoice does. (2) A litigation survey expert or a pharma market-access lead names a live project where a bot-contamination audit was required or would have changed the outcome, or a court excludes a survey over respondent fraud. (3) Written confirmation that SSRS, Verasight and Ipsos do NOT plan to sell standalone audits and will license their control panel to a rival at under $3k per study, with data-use rights for client-facing reports. (4) Signals & Standards or DQC shows no paying per-study buyer after 6-12 months, or one of them agrees to partner or white-label. (5) Evidence that buyers pay for referee services out of their own budget rather than via seller-funded certification, for example an RFP, a procurement mandate or a P&G-style rule requiring a third-party study-level audit. Without (1) or (5), I would treat this as a 1-person methods consultancy riding a free benchmark report, not a company."

objections: NO PROVEN BUDGET, AND BUYERS' REVEALED BEHAVIOR ROUTES AROUND AN AUDITOR. The researcher found no RFP, mandate, or example of anyone paying $3-15k for a per-study audit, and my searches found none either. Buyers who do act push the burden onto suppliers or switch. P&G required its online sample suppliers to hold ISO 20252 certification by 1 July 2025, which buys a standing supplier-side audit and not a per-study referee. The FT drops panels after its own checks and runs in-house trap questions. Co-op asks agencies how they remove bots. After YouGov retracted the Bible Society report, the Bible Society's stated plan was to re-run the survey, with safeguards in place. The price anchors are hostile: buyers haggle $3 down to $2.75 per complete, a 1,000-complete study costs about $3-5k, and a 4x gap between $0.5X and verified $2X sample exists but cheap sample persists. A $3-15k audit is therefore 1-4x the fieldwork bill. GRIT 2026 shows 'Data quality & fraud' named by only 2% of brand-side researchers (n=101, 'topics followed closely', not a budget measure) and supplier fraud-tool use among them down 10%. Caveat: this is absence of evidence plus weak proxies, not proof they will refuse. The pitched $3-15k per-study audit and $50-150k programmes have zero demonstrated payers.

THE CHECK-SIGNER IS UNDEFINED OR CONFLICTED IN EVERY SEGMENT. (a) Insights heads feel the pain but often do not hold the sample line item. Sample is bought by agencies on thin margins, or by clients through price-driven procurement, and one source says some of the largest buyers use software that awards jobs on price. The only neutral-layer adopters I can see for DQC are agencies and suppliers (Sago, Dig Insights, HawkPartners, Advertiser Perceptions). That means the realistic payer is the vendor side, which is the conflict the idea is built to escape. (b) Academic labs buy at about $1.90-2.00 per quality respondent (Prolific, CloudResearch) and are advised to use free checks, so they cannot fund $3-15k. (c) Litigation: a whole Lanham Act survey costs about $15-20k, the dossier found no ruling excluding a survey for bots, and the check would be sold through survey-expert witnesses who field their own panels. (d) Pharma: HCP verification via NPI is already a panel-level feature, with no evidence of an audit premium. Sales cycle is long and relationship-led: generic vendor onboarding runs 2-4 weeks plus legal, security and privacy review before you even get response-level paradata, and I found no market-research-specific cycle data. CAC for a trust product sold to a few hundred buyers will be founder time plus free audits.

THE 'WHITE SPACE' IS SMALLER THAN CLAIMED, AND THE SCARCE ASSET IS OWNED BY THOSE WHO CAN DISINTERMEDIATE YOU. The dossier missed NORC TrueNorth, a calibration service that adjusts opt-in results against the AmeriSpeak probability panel and invites research buyers to email NORC to use it, with NORC's own error-reduction claims (for example 8.6% down to 1.3%). That is a first-party version of 'recalibrate against a known-real control'. Caveat: the page does not discuss fraud or bots and shows no pricing. Logit's Calibr8 is a second calibration offering I could not read. SSRS already productized the parallel probability sample, and Pew published the method free. Signals & Standards (launched 9/2026) sells independent audit with a named personal validation from a former NPD and Toluna chief research officer who sits on IA and GDQ committees. DQC is the neutral scorecard. Verasight sells the verified human reference at about $3.50 per complete and publishes its own Pew replication. Because the control sample is rented, there is no cornered resource, and the 7 Powers analysis finds nothing reachable: no scale, no network effect, no switching costs, and branding requires years of trust the 18-year-old founder does not have. The control-panel owners (NORC, Ipsos, SSRS, Verasight) can sell the 'bias-adjusted estimate' directly, and a reseller adds margin cost, not value, for any buyer who can email NORC.

UNIT ECONOMICS FAIL AT THE PRICE THE MARKET WILL BEAR, AND THE MARKET IS A BOUTIQUE. By the dossier's own arithmetic, a $10k audit leaves roughly 8-38% gross margin (control $2-5k, 25 analyst hours, signals) and a $3k audit loses money, so only $10k+ studies or retainers work. Only the 'high-stakes' tail can pay that, such as litigation, pharma access, and pollsters. The dossier sizes serviceable revenue at $10-25M a year from assumed adoption (15-25% of 150-300 orgs, 500-1,000 high-stakes studies) with no sourced customer count, so even that is soft. It is services-heavy (revenue per head capped by analyst hours), carries E&O and trade-libel exposure from audit stamps and vendor scorecards, and depends on vendors handing over response-level paradata, which raises contract and privacy-consent problems (paradata consent is still debated). Dynata's 2024 Chapter 11 suggests sample economics are thin, so the budgets above it are not generous. Building the 2,000-person address-based panel in the 'first 30 days' is not feasible (about 6% mail response, hundreds of dollars per recruit, low-to-mid six figures). The licensing alternative caps margin and makes the startup dependent on its competitors.

THE PAIN GETS SOLVED CHEAPER, OR SHRINKS, BEFORE AN AUDIT LAYER MATURES. The why-now ('agents beat attention checks') is partly contested: Prolific's CEO reports agent detection at or below 1% outside MTurk, CloudResearch says click farms dominate, and the PNAS agent paper drew a critique preprint. Pew gives no measured prevalence of AI in live polls and says recruitment method matters but is 'not all that matters'. Real, observable fraud (15-30%) is human, and is attacked cheaply: Verisoul at $99-350 a month, Prolific's 100% Human Guarantee (2x refund per flagged agent, with narrow Qualtrics-plus-Prolific eligibility), P&G-style certification, and moving to probability or verified panels, which is the structural answer Pew points to. The 'state of sample quality' marketing engine already exists free: the IA and GDQ H1 2026 benchmark (about 1.8M records, 46 companies) and Pew's study, so the one asset the founder plans to publish is a free commodity from bodies with more data. Synthetic respondents are gaining momentum (GRIT: +18% use among brand-side researchers, Simile raising $200M), which could shrink panel spend and with it the audit pool. Inference, not sourced: an audit tells a buyer after the fact that already-paid-for data is contaminated, which creates blame risk for the insights head who bought it, a weak purchase trigger compared with fixing supplier selection up front.
