Any of these, found before building anything:
1. Pre-commitments. At least 3 of 10 brand-side insights heads (not agencies or vendors) sign a letter of intent or pre-pay at least $10k for a single-study audit, and each can name the budget line and the person who approves it. The dossier's own kill rule is fewer than 3 of 10.
2. A named buyer chain. Evidence that end clients, not agencies or vendors, can and will write an independent third-party audit into supplier contracts, the way P&G wrote ISO 20252 certification into theirs. A mandate from AAPOR, ESOMAR, an ISO standard, or a regulator requiring independent verification would count.
3. A litigation or pharma pull. A survey expert or law firm names a live matter where bot or fraud contamination was challenged or excluded and a client would have paid $10-50k for an independent bias bound, ideally with a ruling or Daubert motion on record.
4. A margin path. A signed licence for a verified or address-based control sample at well under $3k per study, with at least 50% gross margin at a price buyers actually accept. Alternatively, proof that NORC TrueNorth, SSRS and Signals & Standards cannot or will not offer fraud-aware, per-study calibration with error bounds (for example, TrueNorth's team confirming no fraud adjustment and no per-study audit).
5. Hard prevalence data. Independent evidence, not vendor-run, that AI agents are a material share (more than a few percent) of live opt-in traffic, plus a buyer survey showing a willingness to pay a premium for independent verification.
6. A payer who is not conflicted. A paying customer who is not a panel vendor or agency, such as a pollster, journal, or foundation, who wants the signed audit letter.
Absent these, the only defensible form is a solo, fixed-fee consulting practice or a free benchmark used as lead generation, not a venture."

objections: The central white-space claim is false. Per-study ground-truth calibration against an address-recruited panel, run on the same questionnaire, is already a commercial service from the companies that own the scarce control asset. NORC sells TrueNorth, with a case study in 2020, v2.0 in July 2023 and v3.0 in Nov 2024. Projects take 2-5 weeks and cost about 25% less than a full probability study. NORC claims 2/3 to 80% bias reduction. Ipsos KnowledgePanel calibration of opt-in samples appears in PRRI methodology statements for 2021-2023, and DiSogra et al. published the method in 2011. The finalist file's "None ... re-estimates the result against a known-real reference" and the dossier's "white space" both missed this. The dossier already found SSRS, so incumbents with the control sample now hold the mechanism at three firms. The only remaining differentiators are neutrality, a fraud focus (the TrueNorth page I fetched never mentions bots) and a signed stamp. That is a thin wedge, not a product category. The statistics also look shaky. Kennedy and Brick (via a search summary I did not fetch) say modeling is poorly suited to bogus respondents, which are a measurement-error problem. Pew says bogus status is only inferred from proxies and claims no statistical fix. A "contamination-adjusted estimate with error bounds" therefore rests on unidentified assumptions. The control is also not truth: Gallup found careless responding even in its probability panel.

The key input is owned by competitors, and the unit economics fail on both routes. Only NORC, Ipsos, SSRS, Verasight, Gallup and Pew have verified-human panels, and all of them sell sample or calibration. I found no public terms letting a third party resell or license them as a control. Renting a control from a competitor weakens the neutral-referee claim. It also makes your supply depend on a firm that could launch a cheap audit add-on. The dossier's arithmetic gives 8-38% gross margin at $10k per study and a loss at $3k. Building your own address-based panel costs low-to-mid six figures at roughly 6% response, so the finalist file's "first 30 days: recruit ~2,000 humans" is not feasible. Renting a clean verified sample for $3.50-5 per complete also means the control is not scarce, which contradicts the stated non_obvious_insight. A $3-15k audit would also cost 1-4 times the fieldwork bill for a typical 1,000-complete study of $3-5k.

The why-now is weak, and the election-season piece is about to expire. The human-fraud problem is old: Pew documented 4-7% bogus respondents in 2020. A pitch of "remove-flagged is biased and vendors grade themselves" would have worked equally well in 2019-2020, and nobody built a paid per-study referee then. That points to low willingness to pay, not missing supply. This fails the strategy-frameworks why-now test. The AI-agent angle is mostly forward-looking. CloudResearch's own page says organized click farms, not AI agents, are the dominant threat today (fetched and confirmed). The Westwood PNAS result is a lab-built agent, and a critique preprint says it shows no field-level impact. A search summary of a Prolific-funded preprint reports under 1% non-human text across about 4,800 responses at 12 companies. The Bot Olympics has still published no results. Its page says results are due "within weeks", and a June 25 webinar has already passed. The US midterms are Nov 3, 2026, about three weeks out. Enterprise sales cycles of 6-12 months miss that window, and the next presidential cycle is 2028. If agents stay rare, urgency fades. If detection drops to cents per respondent, the audit premium vanishes.

Demand is unproven, and the trust gap is being filled by free or cheaper channels. The dossier found no RFP, mandate or public example of anyone paying $3-15k for a per-study audit, and I found none either. Buyers' revealed responses are to switch suppliers, to insource, or to ask the vendor again, as the Bible Society did. Greenbook GRIT 2026 (fetched, with only the first 100k of 412k characters read) shows brand-side use of "proprietary panels you own" rising 10%. Use of "tools to detect sample fraud from supplier" fell 10%, which does not suggest a growing third-party-check budget. Standards bodies are moving in as well. ISO 20252:2026 strengthens sampling and panel data-quality requirements (Research Live, 1 Sep 2026; fraud is not named, and no transition date is stated). The Insights Association has a 95-question Sample Supply Transparency Framework. Global Data Quality publishes free benchmarks, and Data Quality Co-op sells a 0-1000 Data Trust Score. A former Toluna and NPD chief research officer launched an audit-only practice, Signals & Standards, on 11 Sep 2026. NORC's Neutronian-style certification model also exists in ad data. A free "state of sample quality" benchmark is already published by Pew, GDQ and vendors, so it is not a differentiated marketing engine. The dossier's own serviceable market is about $10-25M, which supports a boutique and not a venture.

Data access and liability make the product hard to deliver and expensive to insure. The audit needs response-level timings, paradata, device data and open-ends. Buyers often do not hold supplier device data, and this is my inference since I found no source on it. Sample is routinely resold through exchanges, aggregators and routers, which the IA's framework itself cites as making participants hard to trace. A per-vendor scorecard can therefore blame the wrong supplier. Vendors have strong reasons to refuse an adversarial auditor raw access. The Op4G/SliceMR indictment alleged about $10M of fake data, with a blog reporting 74 victims, and was followed by 2026 paper retractions. Audit findings are discoverable evidence. Device and paradata sharing also raises GDPR processor-contract limits. A signed "audit stamp" invites professional-liability claims if a stamped study is later retracted. Published vendor scorecards invite trade-libel and false-advertising suits. In fairness, the rating-agency cases I found (BBB, A.M. Best, Moody's, Dun & Bradstreet) mostly turned on qualified privilege and opinion defenses. The real cost is defense spend and E&O premiums for a 1-5 person firm. An audit also sells credentialed trust. No court ruling excluding a survey for bots turned up in either the dossier or my search, so the litigation wedge is still speculative. A first-time founder without methodology credentials would face a cold start against incumbent and veteran-led competitors.

objections: The Stage 1 buyer is already being sold to, in the same workflow, with the opposite commercial shape. Allied RefundPlus pitches repossession, total loss and early payoff 'under one roof' under one MSA, to cut vendor-management and oversight cost, and says outsourcing does not remove the lender's liability. LCT sells 'CU-controlled workflows instead of outsourced models'. Its CUSO is backed by WSECU's CUSO and SWBC, runs 100K+ cancellations a month, has 800+ provider connections, and supports nearly 30 credit unions. LCT is also embedded in AKUVO's credit-union collections platform, so refund requests become 'part of the collection process'. That is exactly the collections-manager buyer this idea targets. F&I Sentinel is wired into Dealertrack and RouteOne. Nobody publishes pricing and I found no one offering contingency. After 4+ years and three funded players, an empty pricing slot is more likely a rejected model than white space. Compliance buyers want one audit trail across payoff, repo and total loss, not a repo/charge-off point solution that fragments it.

'Cash the lender itself keeps' is the wrong frame, and it undermines the 22.5% fee. The refund legally belongs to the consumer and must be applied to the account or deficiency (CFPB, Hudson Cook, and Allied's own FAQ). The lender's real gain is the refund times (1 minus its own collection rate on the deficiency), and zero when the refund exceeds the deficiency. States are shifting the burden onto creditors and assignees (Colorado, NJ, TX), so this is a compliance cost, not found money. Compliance costs get bought as flat-fee or SaaS from the compliance budget, not as a 20-25% cut of member refunds. Wisconsin DFI bars processing fees from being deducted from a customer's refund. VSC refunds are net of claims paid, and several states cap fees (Wisconsin and NC at 10%; Mississippi, Florida and others deduct claims). Contingency also invites two failure modes. Once volume is visible, the lender insources or renegotiates, since contingency carries no recurring commitment. And the lender works the easy files in-house and sends the vendor the hard ones. Lenders also already have a lever the idea ignores: dealer chargebacks and reserve debits.

The unit economics do not clear a credit-union sales motion. The $40-47K per lender per year rests on unsourced or inflated inputs. 1,000 repos per $1B ignores the CFPB's 27% completion rate on repossession assignments and the AFSA claim that 22-30% of repos end with the car returned. It also ignores credit union delinquency of only 81 bps. $700 unearned compares with observed GAP refunds of $165-$380, and VSC refunds shrink after claims and fees. '60% unclaimed' has no source, and incumbents already process 100K+ cancellations a month. My sensitivity (inference): 600 events x 40% with add-ons x $350 x 40% unclaimed x 22.5% = about $7.6K a year per $1B lender, and about $25K even keeping the $700 and 60% inputs. Sales cycles for credit union tech are reported at 6-18 months (blog-grade sources), and vendor due diligence (SOC 2, NCUA third-party review, legal) costs the same whether the contract is worth $8K or $80K. Cash arrives only after onboarding plus an 84-day average administrator cycle. Direct CAC of $30-60K (inference) against $8-25K of at-will contingency revenue means a multi-year payback. The total Stage 1 fee pool is roughly $15-20M by the dossier and lower on corrected inputs. A 5-10% share is under $1-2M.

The first-30-days go-to-market is not executable, and its centerpiece creates the buyer's biggest objection. A free 12-month retrospective audit hands the credit union a written record of past noncompliance. In Colorado, self-audits became settlement terms, with state books-and-records inspection and affidavits to class counsel (Red Rocks, Westerra, Bellco and Canvas). Credit union counsel will want it privileged and run through counsel, which a vendor cannot provide. 'Sign 2 on 25% contingency in weeks 3-4' contradicts the 6-18 month cycle. Contract images carry member PII, so a credit union needs SOC 2-grade evidence, a vendor-risk package and peer references that a new, unreferenced founder lacks (NAFCU and NCUA diligence guidance). Credit unions weight vendor stability and peer validation, and the incumbent CUSO is owned by credit-union-adjacent entities.

Stage 2 and 3 payers have no demonstrated budget, and the demand driver is weakening. Administrators are asked to pay $2-5 per event for intake that scoreboards them and makes their float regulator-visible. Whoever holds unearned premium benefits from slow refunds, so this asks them to buy their own audit. They are already obligated to process cancellations, and the trade associations (GAPA, SCIC and MVPPA) just published refund-portal standards aimed at vendors. F&I Sentinel already links 600+ administrators and LCT 800+, so an 'open schema' competes with those standards and connection libraries. Carriers and reinsurers would pay $50-250K for termination curves, but the dossier found no analog. A dataset of repo and charge-off events from at most about 450 credit unions is a biased sample, because payoffs dominate early termination. F&I Sentinel already sees about 1.75M cancellations a year across payoffs, repos and total loss, so it would own the real curve. Pooled data also raises FCRA questions. Regulators are free, by design. On urgency, the CFPB has retreated and the credit-union-specific signal is fading: NCUA's 2024 priorities named GAP cancellations, but summaries of the 2026 letter (Forvis Mazars) do not mention GAP or add-on refunds. This is an unconfirmed absence; I did not read the letter itself. Credit union repossession growth is also modest next to subprime finance companies.

1. A contingency price from the buyer. At least 3 credit union collections heads, with compliance or counsel sign-off, say in writing that they will pay 20% or more of member refunds on repo and charge-off files. They must prefer that to a flat-fee or SaaS tool, and they must be able to absorb the refund-ownership and exam-optics problem.
2. Pricing from LCT, F&I Sentinel and Allied showing either of two things. They charge high per-event fees that contingency would undercut, or they exclude repo and charge-off files. Today their pricing is undisclosed and Allied lists repo as in scope.
3. Real claim-rate data. A 2-3 credit union pilot shows an average of $300 or more recovered per eligible repo or charge-off file, and a $1B-auto lender nets $30K or more a year in fees. This must be net of VSC claims and fees, dealer chargebacks, and files already recovered in-house.
4. A counsel opinion that a contingency fee on a consumer-owed refund is permissible in the launch states. It would also need to cover a privileged look-back structure that does not create discoverable admissions.
5. A paid pilot, not an LOI, from one administrator or reinsurer for structured loan-end events or termination data. That would prove Stage 2 has a payer.
6. A distribution partner. Origence, a core or LOS vendor, or an existing credit union CUSO or collections platform agrees to resell or embed the desk rather than compete with LCT or Allied.
7. Confirmation that NCUA or state examiners are actively citing repo and charge-off refund failures at $200M-$3B credit unions in 2026. Right now the evidence is Colorado, Massachusetts and older CFPB items.

The most plausible survivor is a bootstrapped, collections-agency-reseller version of Stage 1, with no exchange thesis and a realistic $0.5-2M ceiling."

objections: THE WHY-NOW IS ALREADY OVER AND THE KEY PREMISE IS FALSE. The idea says no one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes. That role has been filled for years. Express Recoveries (F&I Express, around 2017, now owned by F&I Sentinel) describes itself as connecting lenders with providers and dealers on a single platform for cancellation refunds. F&I Sentinel's Managed Cancellations line reportedly covers repossession and charge-off, with 100+ lenders and a network of 600+ administrators, and it was integrated into Dealertrack and RouteOne in January 2026. Allied RefundPlus names repossession and charge-off explicitly and adds a refund lockbox. LCT launched its credit union CUSO on 2026-09-09, one month ago, with WSECU's CUSO, SWBC and AKUVO. AKUVO is a collections platform, so LCT already sits inside the collections workflow and the CUSO channel this idea names as its distribution plan. A new entrant would be 4 to 9 years behind, with no administrator connection library, and would be selling to the same 400 to 450 credit unions. Pure contingency pricing is the only differentiator, and nobody has verified that anyone wants it. Pure contingency also invites adverse selection: lenders with good compliance already use a tool, and lenders without it are the ones with liabilities they won't want surfaced.

THE 'FOUND CASH THE LENDER KEEPS' FRAMING IS LEGALLY WRONG, AND THE FREE AUDIT TURNS INTO A LIABILITY. The refund belongs to the consumer. New Jersey P.L.2019 c.181 §6 puts the duty on the creditor to provide the refund 'without requiring the borrower to request' within 60 days. It lets the creditor apply the refund only to reduce the amount owed on the loan. Hudson Cook's conservative reading is that the holder should refund in all instances. The lender's gain is capped at the outstanding deficiency, and is zero if there is no deficiency or the deficiency is waived or sold. The fee base is much smaller than the model's $190K per $1B lender. Taking 20 to 25% of a statutory consumer refund is poor optics, and Wisconsin DFI bars deducting processing fees from the refund. The free 12-month retrospective audit is worse. Any repossession from the past year that is more than 60 days old without a refund request is a documented statutory miss. The audit hands the lender a written record of its own UDAAP exposure. It also creates a remediation duty to consumers whose deficiencies were already collected, written off or sold. Lender counsel will kill this at the moment it works. The vendor's own work product is probably not privileged. I did not find a source on whether the vendor itself needs a state collection, insurance-producer or administrator license, so that stays an open kill-risk. No one has shown it is clear.

CHARGE-OFF IS THE WRONG TRIGGER, AND THE REFUND ENGINE NEEDS DATA THE LENDER OFTEN DOESN'T HAVE. Statutory clocks run from the termination event, not from charge-off: 60 days in New Jersey, 30 days for the original creditor under Colorado's C.R.S. 5-9.3-106(3), and a 90-day written-request window from the event in New Hampshire and Rhode Island (per search summaries). A monthly batch of repos and charge-offs arrives after those windows have closed, so it is a look-back, which is back to problem 2. State rules differ in ways that make the pro-rata engine hard: a $25 cancellation fee in Colorado, up to $50 in New Jersey, up to 10% in Mississippi, 90% of pro-rata after 60 days in Florida, and balance offset in Nevada. A miscalculation is a UDAAP error for the lender, so the vendor takes on indemnity and E&O demands. On indirect loans, a credit union may hold only a buyer's order with the product name and price, not the product contract with its term and cancellation formula (CUInsight, 2020, possibly dated). LLM contract reading doesn't help when the contract isn't in the file. F&I Sentinel advertises a 190,000-form repository. The 'top 20 administrators and 10 states in two weeks' plan in the 30-day section is not credible against competitors with 600+ administrator links. The lender also has a free lever for indirect loans: debit the dealer's reserve. Ally does this if the dealer doesn't respond within 15 days. That makes paying 22.5% to a vendor hard to justify.

REGULATORY AND TIMING TAILWINDS ARE WEAKER FOR THIS SEGMENT THAN CLAIMED, AND A STARTUP FACES A GATED SALE. The federal retreat reduces federal exam fear: the CFPB dropped its Credit Acceptance case in April 2025 and ended the Toyota Motor Credit order in May 2025. The big state AG action is the $710M Credit Acceptance settlement on 2026-09-17, aimed at a mega subprime lender, not credit unions. Credit union GAP enforcement is concentrated in Colorado (about $23.5M and about 132K borrowers since 2019, mostly payoff refunds, not repossession). The 'record subprime delinquency' story does not describe the target segment: credit union auto delinquency was 80 to 81 bps in Q1 and Q2 2026, flat nationally, and Texas credit unions reported falling delinquency. On sales, NCUA has no direct authority over vendors (the Inspector General said so in 2020), so each credit union does its own due diligence under SL 07-01. A vendor holding contract images (VINs, member data) will face security questionnaires, pen tests and probably SOC 2 before its first sale (the SOC 2 expectation is general practice, not an NCUA requirement). A pure-contingency, zero-upfront model has no cash to pay for any of that. It also means the vendor depends on the lender's own books to know what was recovered, because refunds post to the lender's account and the vendor must trust the lender's reporting to get paid. Allied's lockbox shows that incumbents control the cash flow.

STAGES 2 AND 3 (THE EXCHANGE) HAVE NO VERIFIED PAYER, AND THE STATUTORY-TRIGGER THESIS DOESN'T MATCH THE STATUTES. The New Jersey statute puts the refund duty on the creditor and sets no separate duty or notice requirement for the administrator. Colorado requires the assignee to notify the original creditor, which is typically the dealer, not the administrator. So the claim that administrators can't comply because no one tells them is not a legal gap the law creates. The law makes it the lender's problem, and lender-side tools are the market's answer. Administrators and dealer-owned reinsurers gain from slow or missing refunds (breakage and float), so they are weak payers for $2 to $5 per event. The dossier found no evidence that any administrator pays for lender-attested intake and no analog for $50K to $250K termination-curve data. GAPA, SCIC and MVPPA published refund-portal minimum standards in late 2025 with incumbent vendors involved, so an open schema competes with the standards body and vendors with the connections. Pooling cross-lender loan-end data for sale raises FCRA consumer-reporting-agency and GLBA questions that need counsel before launch. The 5% bull / 60% bear odds in the dossier look generous to the bull case.

objections: WRONG PAYER, UNPROVEN BUDGET. The named buyer (defense associate or partner) does not control the money. The carrier pays the expense invoice and sets the guidelines. The 2026 CLM Litigation Management Study (Insurance Journal, 4/20/2026) found 0% of carriers would contribute to or pay for law-firm tools, 83.1% had never been asked, and only 6.2% use any billing arrangement other than hourly. Ethics opinions describe guidelines where expert and vendor spend needs pre-approval and non-compliant spend is simply not paid (Hawaii 2015). So a $395 kit is either an out-of-pocket cost for a firm billing a squeezed panel rate, or it needs carrier sign-off. Sign-off puts the sales cycle at the carrier, which is the channel the idea says it avoids. The 'priced below the pre-approval threshold' hack rests on a threshold nobody has shown exists. Guideline templates leave the dollar figure blank, it is carrier-specific, and the dossier's own desk search found none. The idea has the reimbursement mechanics backwards.

THE FORCING FUNCTION IS ALREADY SERVED, AND IT IS WEAK WHERE THE WEDGE IS NEW. In Texas, the one place with a mandatory early defense step (the 18.001 counteraffidavit), MedCost Contain, No World Borders and IMS Legal already sell signed-coder affidavits, and In re Allstate held that a nurse-CPC suffices, so the signature is a commodity there. The Texas Supreme Court also said a missing counteraffidavit does not stop a defendant from contesting reasonableness at trial, so even that spend is optional. HB 2446 (the $50k affidavit-sufficiency bill) was received by the Senate on 5/12/2025 and the legislative history shows no further action, so Texas has no new trigger. Georgia has no affidavit regime. O.C.G.A. 24-9-921 lets the patient identify bills and says no expert is needed to show reasonableness, so a defense expert is a discretionary cost. SB 68's medical-expense rules cover only causes of action arising on or after 4/21/2025, so treating-provider depositions on qualifying files will mostly arrive in 2027 (my inference from the 2-year limitations period). The 'why now' is a Georgia story that has not yet produced files.

THE PRODUCT'S PAYOFF IS WEAKLY EVIDENCED, AND THE VALUE LANDS AT THE CARRIER, NOT THE LAWYER. Cross-examination kits and testimony matter only on files that reach depositions and trial. About 1.25% of litigated BI cases reached verdict in 2025, versus roughly 12% in 2016. A Georgia plaintiff firm's juror polling says jurors who accept necessity do not debate price. An LSU Law Review note says billing experts cannot change awards in Louisiana. Young v. Panera (M.D. Fla. 2024) excluded a defense coding expert and the plaintiff's proof of reasonableness survived post-trial. Both the dossier and the idea assume the 'testimony is the profit center' attach rate is 10-15%. Nothing supports that number, and Georgia exclusion risk (11th Cir. district courts) cuts directly against it. The real settlement-leverage value accrues to the adjuster, who already buys bill-line analysis from Enlyte and similar vendors and hands it down with the file. That makes the lawyer's willingness to pay for the same analysis near zero.

THE $395 CORE IS COMMODITIZING AND THE MARGIN LAYER IS SELF-IMPEACHING. USLAW's Summer 2026 magazine describes defense lawyers already loading pleadings, records and bills into closed AI systems to generate deposition outlines. The dossier concedes the know-how is public (ALFA publishes the cross topics). What a general LLM cannot give is the signature, and that is the piece already commoditized in Texas and exclusion-prone in Georgia. The model also contradicts itself. Kits are the funnel and testimony is the margin, so the coder's repeat-defense-business interest is exactly the bias attack the kit teaches counsel to run on the treating doctor. A 25-minute review before a coder signs a document meant for deposition use is an easy cross question ('how long did you spend?'). The $40-90 marginal cost and 25-minute figures are the founder's own unverified estimates.

ECONOMICS: UNREACHABLE LIST, NO VALIDATED PRICE POINT, AND FRONT-LOADED FIXED COST. No source validates $395, the $3-5k expert-premium premise, $1,900 declarations, or the 5 kits per firm per month (my guess is that figure is high, because only files with LOP treatment that reach a treating-provider deposition qualify). The dossier found no count of 3-20 lawyer defense boutiques (its 80-150 firm figure is inference), and some of the reachable BI defense work is in-house at carriers with staff counsel (Allstate, Progressive and Root post Texas BI trial-attorney roles), which has captive vendor channels. The ceiling is about $24k/month at 12 firms and a $3-5M SAM at 100 firms. Before the first dollar the plan needs two state-specific testifying coders, contractor coders, an ex-panel-counsel advisor, E&O cover, Daubert-defense readiness and a Context4-or-TiC data build. TiC anchors may be blank for many LOP providers, since LOP care often bypasses insurance networks. The plan funds all of that from 3-5 converted firms at $395 per kit after a free first kit and a founder-run 15-call sales process. Sales cycles for carrier-approved or panel-gated purchases are slow, and CAC is paid in founder hours against a customer set with no list.

Homeowners who pay already spent $3k-$17k on testing, and 75% were underinsured. Finch ($4.5M raised, sells to PAs) already owns the PA inbox and can add an IH-report module. The 'PA tier' is 15-25 firms, so $395 times a realistic 120-650 audits is $47k-$257k a year. That is nowhere near the pitched $1.5M-$2.5M.

The $40k-$150k plaintiff-analytics tier is effectively one buyer with two better alternatives. Both Ghazarian-type class actions and the State Farm/EFI suit came from one firm, Singleton Schreiber. In discovery that firm can compel the defendant vendor's own report files and sampling data. A retained testifying CIH then does the pattern analysis, because software output is not testimony. Legal-AI vendors sell by demo, per-case quote and SOC2 or security review. That sales cycle is months, not the 'one attorney LOI for a 100-report pilot at about $25k' inside 30 days. No class-action ruling, such as demurrer or certification, was found. The tier is also a single-point-of-failure revenue line, and it is the line the bottom-up depends on.

The timing window closes before the go-to-market can mature, and the pool shrinks monthly. Suits on the 2025 fires are generally due by about 1/7/2027 (Ins. Code 2071's 24 months, tolling argued). The 30-day plan reaches the first paid audit in week 4, with only 25 reports and 90% field-level accuracy, and then has about 8 weeks to sell to professionals who already have experts. AB 1795 only governs new claims from 1/1/2027, and no large urban fire is scheduled. CDI's July 2026 data show about 98% of residential claims in both fires have at least one payment (not the same as closed). SCE's wildfire compensation program, where about half of claims are smoke, soot or ash non-burn damage, offers a payer that bypasses the carrier IH dispute for Eaton. The Grid is also a depreciating asset: the research flags conflicting dates for state standards (end-2028/2029 versus 7/2027), and PAs on smoke claims must have state training and certification under the digest. Event-driven revenue means little repeat purchase and a lumpy, short-lived LTV.

Delivery depends on scarce licensed CIHs at uneconomic rates, which breaks the margin or the credibility. The CIH-signed plan nets about $450 per plan, which is three hours or less at $150 per hour. The older IH canons say to sign only work prepared by the IH or under their direction and control, so a CIH cannot just stamp a vendor-drafted plan. The CIH must effectively redo it, which is the $2k-$4k engagement the product claims to undercut. CIHs are the stated bottleneck (Kennedys and Brocksmith both flag hygienist and lab capacity). Carriers are racing to expand certified-hygienist rosters, so the best CIHs have better-paying demand. Add E&O exposure and the chance that a PA's letter touches unlicensed adjusting or unauthorized practice of law. Add 1-1.5 hours of human QA at $60-$150 an hour per audit plus the two CIHs and toxicologist the 30-day plan buys. First-month revenue (30 audits, about $11.9k) roughly equals first-month expert cost. The 'largest labeled dataset' moat is weak too: Purdue holds 518+ files, is NSF-funded to Jan 2029, and plans a free public AI report-reader.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Hard purchase evidence, not interest. Specifically: (1) At least 5 of 10 PAs or coverage attorneys with live, disputed standing-home files pay the full $395 for a second audit after a free first one, and at least 2 report the carrier or FAIR Plan authorized more testing after receiving the scorecard letter. (2) A litigation firm signs a paid pilot with a signed SOW of $25k or more. An LOI does not count, and neither does a pilot that needs the vendor's own discovery documents. (3) Two policyholder-side CIHs, under their own direction-and-control standard, agree to sign supplemental plans at $450 or less, or agree to buy the tool as workflow software at a price that clears the gross-margin math. (4) The chaptered AB 1795/AB 1642 text or implementing guidance shows a defined sampling-plan requirement, or applies to open 2025-fire claims, which would turn the letter from persuasion into a statutory demand. (5) Purdue/Tufts/UCLA confirm in writing that their AI report-reader stays explanatory, produces no claim-ready deliverable, and will not launch before mid-2027. (6) A count of at least 1,000 open, PA- or attorney-represented, disputed standing-home claims. I would then also accept a reframe as policyholder-side CIH workflow software (extraction plus gap list, sold to scarce testifying experts), because it removes the signature and buyer-wants-an-expert problems. That is a smaller, differently priced business than the one pitched.

objections: TIMING: the AB 1795 why-now mostly does not reach the customers in the wedge, and the window is closing from three sides. (a) One policyholder-side reading says the testing-payment section (2060.2) is expressly limited to claims on or after its operative date, while the ALE section (2060.1) is arguable for existing claims. Other sources say insurer inspection is elective, and Kennedys' Sipple says impact-zone status does not compel identical testing in every home. So an 'AB 1795 deficiency letter' on the Jan 2025 fires is a persuasive benchmark, not a statutory demand, and the dossier never read the chaptered text. (b) The Eaton half of the wedge has a parallel payer. SCE's Wildfire Recovery Compensation Program takes non-burn smoke, soot and ash claims, reportedly with no additional documentation inside the eligibility area. About half of its 4,000+ claims are non-burn, and submissions close Nov 30, 2026, before this product could ship. (c) By CDI's July 2026 table about 98% of 38,737 residential claims already had a payment. The live disputes are a small tail, and the biggest ones are about remediation scope, not sample count: Farmers paid about $80k against a more-than-$1M demolition recommendation, and $135k against $1.5M. A $395 omission list does not decide a $1M scope fight, and those claimants hire CIHs and litigation experts. (d) Real volume after 2027 needs a new urban conflagration with standing smoke-damaged homes. That is lumpy, and no other state has a comparable statute. The pitch's own 'we survive the standard' argument also fails, because the Grid's differentiator disappears once DTSC and CalEPA publish sampling and screening standards. Dates conflict across sources: April drafts said 2027, CalMatters says end-2028 for lead and asbestos and end-2029 for other contaminants.

REGULATION AND LIABILITY sit on the exact deliverables. The product ships a statute-cited deficiency letter plus a sampling plan a CIH signs. (a) Unauthorized practice of law: In re Reynoso (9th Cir. 2007, 477 F.3d 1117) held, under California law, that a web-based tool producing customized document suggestions went beyond clerical help and was unauthorized practice of law. The State Bar is separately reviewing whether legal-AI products need regulation. The dossier flagged the $295 direct-to-homeowner tier but treats selling to PAs as 'safer'. It is not obviously safer, because a licensed PA sending LLM-drafted statutory legal-position letters is the person exposed, and in other states PAs preparing statutory notices have been treated as practicing law. Ins. Code 15006/15007 licensing also applies to anyone who 'aids' an insured in negotiating. (b) AB 1795 reportedly requires CDI to build adjuster and public-adjuster training and certification by 7/1/2029, and says uncredentialed adjusters cannot handle these claims. That adds a compliance layer on the buyer's side, and the dossier left the scope unverified. (c) A CIH of record who signs a plan drafted by software takes personal licence-and-ethics risk and malpractice exposure on a $450 half-fee, and this is also the scarce-labor bottleneck for a 48-hour SLA. (d) Expert admissibility: California's Sargon 'analytical gap' doctrine means an LLM scorecard needs a human expert sponsor, which pushes the buyer back to a testifying CIH. (e) The plaintiff-analytics line ($40k-$150k, the largest revenue assumption) needs hundreds of reports that are discovery material, probably under protective orders, or privileged work product. A third-party vendor ingesting them needs consulting-expert status, and those plaintiffs get the vendor's whole report population by discovery anyway.

TECHNICAL: there is no authoritative yardstick, and the inputs are messier than the 25-report pilot assumes. The Grid is self-authored, and its main citations cut against the pitch. The AIHA guide authors told the CDI task force that targeted sampling against background is correct and exhaustive sampling is unnecessary, so a scorecard that penalizes low sample counts invites a rebuttal quoting AIHA. Purdue's review of hundreds of reports found sampling and recommendations 'vary widely': metal loadings reported as ug/wipe, ug/sqft or ug/100cm2, conflicting lead standards (EPA 5 vs CDPH 10 ug/sqft), no-detect wipes paired with 'remediate' recommendations, and different VOC panels per vendor. Field-level extraction above 90% on 25 curated reports will not hold across dozens of vendor templates, scans and tape-lift photos. Judging 'comparison basis' and 'necessity' is expert judgment, not extraction. Human QA at 1-1.5 hours plus CIH review on a $395, 48-hour product leaves thin or negative margin once errors are corrected, and an error that sinks a claim is E&O exposure.

COMMODITIZATION AND SUNSET: no durable power, and a free substitute is arriving. The Grid is deliberately public and cited, and extraction plus gap-listing against public guides is the thing a frontier LLM does for a PA or attorney today for pennies. The 'largest labeled dataset' claim is wrong: Purdue/Tufts/UCLA already hold 500+ submitted reports (versus the plan's 25) and share with CDI. The Purdue NSF platform is early-stage, with co-design still to come and funding to 2029. That makes it a pricing anchor and a free-alternative risk timed to the product's maturity, not an imminent launch (the dossier's 'High' near-term threat is somewhat overstated). Finch ($4.5M, 9/29/2026) owns the PA inbox and can add an IH-report module. Counter-positioning against HygieneTech or Rimkus is moot, because they were never going to build this, so it is not a 7 Powers advantage. The only plausible durable asset is the CIH network and attorney trust, which is a services business.

UNIT ECONOMICS AND BUYER DEPTH: the reachable market is thin and concentrated. The wedge is 15-25 PA firms plus 3-5 plaintiff firms, and Singleton Schreiber brought both class actions and the State Farm/EFI suit. PA software prices at $99-$250 a month (ClaimWizard), which undercuts the $2,500 a month plan. Remaining disputed, PA-represented files are an estimated 1,200-3,250, nobody has shown a PA, attorney or carrier purchase, and no evidence shows a deficiency letter changes carrier behavior. Realistic year one is about $0.1M-$0.5M versus the pitched $1.5M-$2.5M, with most of the upside resting on unvalidated analytics contracts. Suit-limitation pressure around 1/7/2027 may make demand spiky and also early, before a v0.1 Grid, two CIH reviews and consented reports exist. Realistic launch is Dec-Jan.

objections: The profit center (testimony) is a commodity in the one state where it is forced, and a Daubert liability in the other. In Texas, In re Allstate (2021) let a nurse with billing-review experience sign a counteraffidavit that need not meet trial admissibility standards. Coder-signature shops (MedCost Contain, No World Borders, IMS Legal) already sell that layer, so the signature is not scarce there. In Georgia and the 11th Circuit the signature is scarce, but for a reason: Young v. Panera (M.D. Fla. 2024) excluded a defense coding expert on reasonable value. Plaintiffs argue coders are generally unqualified on reasonable charges. I found no Georgia appellate ruling admitting a coder on reasonable value after SB 68 (the dossier found none either). Efficacy is also doubtful: a Louisiana law review note argues billing experts cannot move awards, and a Georgia plaintiff firm says jurors rarely fight over price once treatment is deemed necessary. The 10-15% kit-to-testimony attach rate has no evidence behind it. 'Kits as funnel, testimony as margin' hands the plaintiff a bias cross: the coder is a repeat defense vendor paid by the file. The 'compounding cornered resource' also belongs to the named coder personally. That coder can leave with the track record or demand the margin.

The 'price below the carrier pre-approval threshold' distribution hack is unsupported, and it probably fails on the payer/user split. The dossier found no threshold, and I found none. What I did find is the opposite pattern: carrier panel guidelines condition payment on approval for expert retention (The Hartford's panel guidelines say many of its policies require prior approval; that quote comes from a search summary, because my fetch of the page timed out). A Rhode Island ethics opinion states that non-compliance with guidelines means non-payment. A coder-signed kit with a testimony option is an expert or consultant retention, not a small disbursement under a dollar line. If the carrier will not reimburse an unapproved $395, the associate pays it from the firm's margin on every file, and the 5 kits per month per firm in the revenue model falls to near zero. Defense lawyers also bill hourly, so a tool that cuts their cross-prep time has no natural budget line. Ethics opinions calling pre-approval rules improper (RI 1999, Ohio 2000) are from 1998-2000, and the dossier cites them as if they were current practice. The real buyer is the carrier, which is the channel the pitch says it avoids.

The core production method, LLM pre-code plus a 25-minute coder sign-off, is the exact fact pattern courts and commentators are flagging in 2025-26. Kohls v. Ellison (D. Minn. Jan. 2025) excluded an entire expert declaration because of unverified AI output, even though the errors were 'innocent'. Matter of Weber (N.Y. Sur. Ct. 2024) refused to blindly accept AI-performed calculations. Law-firm guidance now tells experts to disclose the tool, version, tasks and verification steps, and to keep prompts and outputs. A $1,900 signed declaration produced in 25 minutes with a model is therefore the first thing plaintiffs will probe on cross, and the cost advantage becomes the exhibit. Proposed FRE 707 was reportedly sent back for more work in June 2026 (one law-firm source), so there is no clear rule to rely on. The workflow also moves the plaintiff's medical records into a vendor's LLM pipeline. HIPAA qualified protective order templates cover 'consultants' and 'other entities' in the litigation but say nothing about AI vendors, and they carry return-or-destroy duties. The Heppner ruling (S.D.N.Y.) found privilege waived through a public AI tool. Defense counsel carry the Rule 1.6 and 5.3 duties, so each firm will need QPO language, zero-retention terms and no-training terms before uploading anything. That is a slow sales cycle for a $395 product. E&O and UPL exposure were not researched by the dossier, and I did not resolve them either.

The data anchors are either unavailable for LOP providers or free elsewhere. The TiC 'same TIN's negotiated rates' anchor exists only where the LOP provider sits in a payer network, and LOP treatment is typically chosen to bypass insurance. The dossier flags 'blank anchors' as an inference and I found no coverage data. No court was found accepting TiC rates as proof of reasonable value, and the In re Allstate-approved method used a UCR database. Building the anchor is expensive. Payer files run up to about 1 TB each and are refreshed monthly. Serif and Turquoise sell cleaned data as enterprise subscriptions, and Turquoise bars linking its data to other transparency vendors. The CMS final rule published Oct 6, 2026 will change file contents within about 5 months, so any in-house pipeline faces rework. CPT code descriptors are AMA-licensed: the AMA says a license is required for products distributed by a vendor, and it works through distributors with royalties. The $40-90 marginal cost ignores both costs. The kit's other 'unique' inputs are available free through the case itself. Florida and Georgia statutes force disclosure of the LOP, the referral source and the factoring price. In Texas, In re K&L Auto Crushers (2021) and In re ExxonMobil let defendants subpoena the very provider's negotiated rates from insurers, a better anchor than TiC. What remains is packaging.

The why-now is partly misframed, and the audit layer is commoditizing underneath the pitch. Texas has no new forcing statute: SB 30 died, and HB 2446 (affidavit alone sufficient) passed the House and reached the Senate on May 12, 2025, with no further action shown on the bill history page. Georgia SB 68's medical-expense section applies only to causes of action arising on or after April 21, 2025, so contested treating-provider depositions at volume arrive around 2027, and a first-year revenue plan is built on volume that does not exist yet. The reforms also attack the problem the product sells against. Florida-style caps tie evidence to paid amounts, which should push plaintiffs and providers away from LOP billing, but I found no post-reform usage data either way. The line-item audit is already sold at kit prices: MedLegal AI advertises a defense-side billing audit (upcoding, unbundling, duplicate billing) at $200-500 per case with turnaround in hours, and publishes guides for prompting a generalist LLM to do the same work. The only remaining differentiator is the credentialed signature, which objection 1 shows is the weakest piece. The dossier's own SAM is about $3-5M a year across roughly 80-150 firms (an inference), which cannot fund two retained testifying coders, a CPT and data license, E&O and a founder. The founder, an 18-year-old with no clinical, coding or legal credentials, would be selling a 'credentialed expert' product to defense lawyers through calls he must make while managing school and admissions.

result.title: Repo-Day Refund Desk (residual of the Auto Loan-End Event Exchange)
result.one_liner: A same-week, flat-fee desk that recovers and tracks unearned add-on refunds on repossession, total-loss and payoff events for small non-bank auto lenders and servicers that are legally pushed to fix this and have no tool. The exchange is deleted.
result.pitch:
Verdict: dead as pitched. The exchange (Stages 2-3) was the only venture-scale part, and it is pre-empted: F&I Express launched the same lender-to-provider cancellation network in 2017 behind Dealertrack, Cox bought it and in Jan 2024 sold it as an "important, niche post-sale function", and no administrator is shown to pay for it. The lender-side desk is already sold by three funded vendors (Allied RefundPlus, which lists repossession and charge-off; LCT, whose CUSO has about 30 credit unions; F&I Sentinel, which runs a managed service "from trigger to resolution"). Percent-of-refund pricing is also wrong: the refund belongs to the consumer and has to be credited to the deficiency.

What survives is narrow. Sell to lenders who must act and have no tool: state-licensed non-bank auto lenders and their third-party servicers, for example those in the Massachusetts 2024 consent orders, which required a look-back to Dec 2018. Sell a paid, counsel-engaged look-back, then a go-forward desk driven by a daily event feed. Use a flat fee per paid event and drop the free audit. There is no moat at launch, no proven differentiation, and a realistic ceiling of about $0.5-2M a year. I would not build it unless the two-week test finds unserved lenders who will name a price.
result.wedge_customer: State-licensed independent auto finance companies and third-party servicers with about $50M-$500M in receivables, no refund vendor, and exam or consent-order exposure. The secondary channel is credit-union recovery CUSOs and collection agencies that already hold lender relationships and could resell. Credit-union collections managers are dropped as the direct first buyer, because LCT, Allied and F&I Sentinel already sell to them.
result.first_product: Two parts. (1) A paid look-back for lenders under a mandate, engaged through the lender's outside counsel so privilege is possible. (2) A go-forward desk fed by a daily repossession, total-loss and payoff feed or forwarded emails, not a monthly batch. It reads the deal jacket with an LLM, picks the administrator and state rule, computes the refund, files the cancellation, tracks it to payment, and gives the lender a posting report and audit trail. A human reviews every file at first. Charge-off is handled only as a look-back or backstop.
result.pricing: Flat $40-$90 per paid cancellation (no refund recovered, no fee), $5-10K per counsel-engaged look-back project, and a small annual minimum. No percentage of consumer refunds, and no free audit. This now looks like incumbent pricing (their pricing is undisclosed), so price is not a differentiator.
result.why_now: Real but shared with every vendor. State rules and enforcement are tightening: Colorado C.R.S. 5-9.3-106 (Jan 2024), NJ P.L.2019 c.181, California AB 2311, the Massachusetts orders (Nov 2024), and the roughly $710M Credit Acceptance multistate settlement (Sept 2026). LLM extraction of deal-jacket documents cuts per-file cost. The federal retreat shifts enforcement to states but gives an entrant no edge over incumbents. Credit-union auto delinquency is flat at 81 bps, so the credit-union segment is weak. The non-bank segment is the stronger driver (unverified).
result.moat: None reachable with confidence. Counter-positioning fails because a success-fee tier is a one-line change for F&I Sentinel or LCT, and it is legally awkward. Scale, network and cornered-resource advantages belong to incumbents (a 190,000-form repository, 600-800+ administrator connections, CUSO equity). The only plausible power is modest switching costs, once the audit trail is embedded in the servicing workflow for 12+ months, plus a small deal-jacket-to-refund corpus. The honest rating is "no power at launch, weak switching costs later".
result.bottom_up_market: Credit-union segment (inference): about 450 CUs with $200M+ in auto loans, from NCUA Q2 2026 data of $485.4B auto, 4,214 CUs and 748 over $500M in assets. Annual fee per $1B-auto CU is about $7.6K (low), $25K (mid) or $42.5K (the idea's own inputs). That gives a pool of about $3.4M, $11M or $19M. The dossier's $15-20M uses the inflated inputs. A 5-10% share after three years, against LCT, Allied and F&I Sentinel, gives about $0.2-1.9M a year, central $0.6-1.1M. Direct CAC of $30-60K (unsourced) against $8-25K a year of at-will revenue has a 2-7 year payback, so direct credit-union sales do not clear. Non-bank segment: the Fed (Experian Velocity 2022) puts non-captive finance companies at about 10% and buy-here-pay-here at about 6% of auto originations. I found no count of firms. An illustrative $200M-receivable lender could yield about $40-100K a year, but that is unverified, and the reachable count is what the test must establish.
result.competitors_and_edge: Competitors, all funded and ahead. F&I Sentinel (Calera-backed; Express Recoveries and a managed cancellations service; Dealertrack and RouteOne integrations Jan 2026; reportedly 150+ lenders and 600+ administrators). LCT (Refund Control, 800+ provider connections; CUSO launched Sept 2026 with WSECU's parent, AKUVO's CEO and SWBC; embedded in AKUVO's collections platform). Allied RefundPlus (repossession and charge-off, lockbox, NAFCU Preferred Partner). No competitor pricing is public, and no contingency or success-fee tier was found. Edge, honestly: none proven. Candidates are segment focus on non-bank lenders and servicers (unverified), event-time handling, counsel-engaged look-backs for mandated buyers, and white-labeling through agencies. All of them are copyable.
result.riskiest_assumption: A reachable group of lenders exists that (a) currently leaves repossession and charge-off add-on refunds unworked, (b) is not already served by LCT, Allied or F&I Sentinel, and (c) has a budget owner who will pay a new, unreferenced vendor a named price.
result.two_week_test: About $500 and 60 hours. Days 1-3: build a coverage map. Take lenders from NCUA call-report data (auto balances of $200M or more), state licensee lists and public consent orders, and subtract those publicly tied to LCT's CUSO, Allied or F&I Sentinel. Gate: at least 150 named reachable lenders with no public incumbent tie. Days 3-14: hold 15 disclosed-research calls (8 non-bank lenders or servicers, 5 CU collections or compliance heads, 2 agency or CUSO partners). Ask who handles repossession and charge-off refunds, which vendor, what they pay, what share of recent repossessions with add-ons got a refund, the last exam finding, who owns the budget, and their reaction to flat versus percentage pricing. Add a 1-hour consumer-finance counsel consult ($300-600) on the fee structure, vendor licensing, and a counsel-engaged look-back. Pass: at least 6 of 15 have no vendor and no systematic process; at least 3 sign a non-binding LOI naming a price (flat $40 or more per event, or 20% or more contingency) and a budget owner; at least 1 channel partner requests a pilot; counsel sees no license or fee blocker. Kill: fewer than 3 of 15 are unserved, most cite an incumbent or in-house process, or counsel blocks the model.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: All three critiques are conceded on their core points, and the idea is judged not alive. Exchange (all three critics): deleted. F&I Express launched the same network in 2017, and Cox sold it in Jan 2024 as a "niche post-sale function". That is slightly softer than "dumped as non-core", but still shows no platform business. There is no administrator payer, and GAPA/SCIC/MVPPA standards and incumbent connection libraries already exist. No open schema, carrier data or settlement layer remains. Lender desk: I verified that F&I Sentinel runs a managed "trigger to resolution" service, Allied lists repossession and charge-off, and nobody discloses pricing or a contingency tier. The contingency differentiator is gone and the free audit is deleted. The audit becomes a paid, counsel-engaged look-back sold only to buyers already under a mandate such as the Massachusetts Ironhorse order. Legal frame: the pitch is liability reduction, the refund is credited to the consumer's deficiency, and pricing is flat per paid event with no percentage of consumer money. Vendor licensing stays an open kill-risk and goes to counsel. Trigger: repossession, total-loss and payoff events handled same-week, not charge-off batches. Economics: recomputed to $7.6K / $25K / $42.5K per $1B CU and a $3-19M pool. One partial pushback: the critics' $165-$380 refund benchmark comes mostly from early payoffs, so repossession refunds may be larger. A secondhand $1,700 figure is untraceable, so per-file value is uncertain by about 5x and is not proven tiny. That does not rescue the sales cycle, the incumbents or the missing moat. Net: no moat, no proven wedge, a $0.5-2M ceiling. The only live question is whether unserved, compelled non-bank buyers exist, and the two-week test answers it.

result.title: Blind Test Lab for Survey-Fraud Defenses
result.one_liner: A neutral lab that sends labeled fake and real respondents through survey-fraud tools and panel suppliers and publishes how many fakes got in and how many real people were wrongly removed, paid for by the sell side that needs proof.
result.pitch:
Online survey sellers grade their own homework. Every fraud-defense claim in market research ("we catch 100% of AI agents", "our panel is clean") comes from a vendor testing its own product: CloudResearch's roughly 1,000-completion white paper, Verisoul's internal tests, Prolific's guarantee. The industry's answer so far is process paperwork: ISO 20252 certificates and a 95-question Insights Association self-disclosure framework (Aug 2026) that nobody verifies. The IA itself said its ISO 27001 audit would not have caught the Op4G fraud.

This business is the independent test lab. It runs blind, pre-registered tests with labeled traffic. Agents at several sophistication levels, scripted fraud personas and 100-150 verified real humans go through a detection tool or a supplier's live registration and survey path. We report two numbers with confidence intervals: how much known-fake traffic leaked in, and how many verified humans were wrongly removed (Pew showed that cleaning itself biases results). We inject the labels, so ground truth is known by construction. That removes the need for a 2,000-person probability panel and for unidentifiable "contamination-adjusted estimates".

Money follows the one flow that already exists here: sellers pay referees (Dynata to Neutronian, suppliers to CIRQ, P&G requiring ISO 20252). The first customers are challenger detection vendors who must contest incumbents' self-tested claims. They pay $4.5-8k for a private red-team report. Panel suppliers come next, at $9k for an annual test. The public quarterly benchmark is free, in the AV-Comparatives style: fees buy depth and logo rights, never results.

This is a small, trust-gated lab, not a venture. Realistic year-3 revenue is $0.15-0.6M, and it dies fast if no one will put a deposit on a test. That test costs under $600 and takes two weeks.
result.wedge_customer: The founder or head of product at an independent challenger survey-fraud detection vendor (dtect, Roundtable, ReDem, Obsurvant, CleanID or DeviceForensIQ-type; roughly 6-8 firms). These firms lose deals to incumbents' self-tested "we catch 100%" claims. They sign from a product or R&D budget with no procurement cycle, and dtect already offers a free 30-day pilot. The private failure analysis is useful R&D, so the first dollar does not depend on end buyers demanding evidence. The second customer is the head of quality or operations at a mid-size panel or sample aggregator, the person who already signs ISO 20252/CIRQ spend. Insights heads who buy sample, academic labs, litigators, pharma and pollsters are dropped as customers.
result.first_product: A pre-registered, blind "labeled-traffic" benchmark round, published free as a quarterly public report, plus a paid private red-team report for each tested tool. Test design: attack tiers T0 scripted speeder, T1 LLM text via API, T2 browser-using commercial agent, T3 agent with anti-detect browser and residential proxy, and D duplicate-identity multi-account. Plus 100-150 rented verified humans. Output per tool is the leak rate per tier and the false-removal rate, each with exact confidence intervals, issued as a dated measurement report rather than an "audit stamp". Safeguards: vendor-signed configuration before any run, a 14-day factual-correction window with no veto, a named methodologist co-signer, consent in writing before touching any production system, and evasion recipes withheld. These are the lessons from the NSS Labs vs CrowdStrike dispute. It measures resistance to known attack classes, not prevalence of fraud in a supplier's real traffic.
result.pricing: Sell-side pays. The public benchmark is free and published regardless of who pays (AV-Comparatives analog: fees buy services, retests and logo licences, never results). Private red-team report for a detection vendor: $4.5k per tool per round, including failure analysis by attack tier, a 60-day retest and a citation and logo licence. Supplier test: $9k per year (about 450 agent sessions plus 150 human controls through registration, profile and survey paths, with a leak and false-removal report, a remediation memo and an attestation letter shareable under NDA), plus a $3k retest at 6 months. Later, a marketplace or aggregator rolling programme at $30-60k per year (untested assumption). Estimated margins: 43-63% on a supplier test at $9k, around 75% on a shared-round vendor report at $4.5k. These come from my arithmetic on rented-sample prices and an imputed $75-150 hourly rate, with no insurance quote yet.
result.why_now: 1) Every accuracy claim is self-tested. CloudResearch's 1,000-completion test was on its own product, Verisoul claims 100% from internal tests, and the Bot Olympics (CloudResearch site, MIT judges) still says "Coming Soon" with no results. I found no independent labeled head-to-head benchmark of survey-fraud tools in one search, which is not proof none exists. 2) The industry just built self-disclosure frameworks without verification. The IA Sample Supply Transparency Framework (Aug 29, 2026) has 95 questions and no mention of audits or testing. ISO 20252:2026 tightens panel data-quality requirements. P&G made ISO 20252 a supplier obligation in July 2025. The IA said ISO 27001 would not have caught Op4G, so process certificates do not test whether data are real. 3) Attacker traffic is now commodity. Westwood's agent produced fake responses at about five cents each, so a red-team harness is cheap to build and the scarce part is credible neutral measurement. The "agents are rampant" story is contested (Prolific at or below 1%, CloudResearch says click farms dominate), so the product also tests scripted and human-style fraud personas and does not depend on that claim. The election hook and human-fraud-is-new framing are dropped.
result.moat: Honest answer: no power today, because the tests are copyable and the human controls are rentable. Reachable powers, in order. (1) Counter-positioning: the lab owns no sample and no detection IP, so CloudResearch, Prolific, Verasight, Verisoul, Ipsos, NORC and SSRS cannot referee themselves. Signals & Standards and DQC are already neutral, so this is a partial win only. (2) Scale economy in the harness: the labeled corpus and attack library are fixed costs spread over every tool and supplier tested, which is small but real. (3) A weak cornered resource: a private held-out attack-trace library that vendors must not see, since a vendor cannot hold a credible private test set about itself. (4) Switching costs later: a longitudinal track record of a supplier's results does not transfer to another lab. (5) Branding or standard-setting is the only power that makes this a company. It is reached only by publishing the protocol and becoming the reference test method for the IA/GDQ, ISO 20252 certifiers or AAPOR, plausibly 2-4 years and not guaranteed. Without that adoption it stays a boutique.
result.bottom_up_market: Year-3 realistic, bottom-up. The dossier's $10-25M assumed buyer-paid high-stakes audits, which are now dropped. (a) Independent detection vendors: about 8 reachable, named in the competition file, of which 3-5 buy 1-2 rounds at $4.5-8k, giving $15-60k. (b) Suppliers and aggregators: Cint alone self-reports 800+ suppliers and 4,600+ panels (its ESOMAR answers), mostly tiny. My unsourced assumption is that 150-300 have real quality teams and 5-10% adopt at about $12k including the retest, giving 8-30 customers and $90-360k. (c) Marketplaces and large agencies: an assumed 5-10 exist and 1-3 sign at $30-60k, giving $30-180k. Total is about $0.15-0.6M per year. The ceiling is low single-digit $M, and only if a certifier, the IA or ISO 20252 adopts the protocol. Year-1 plausible revenue is $0-60k, with a base case near $35k (4 vendor reports plus 2 supplier tests). My judgment is a 10-15% chance of reaching $100k a year and a 3-5% chance of becoming the reference standard. Those odds are not computed. Customer counts other than the Cint figure and the named vendors are assumptions.
result.competitors_and_edge: CloudResearch/MIT Bot Olympics: an open red-team vs blue-team contest hosted by a conflicted vendor. Details and results are unpublished, and if MIT releases an open labeled dataset it is a free input as well as a threat. Data Quality Co-op: passive signal aggregation and a 0-1000 Trust Score embedded in Sago, Dig Insights and Advertiser Perceptions. We test whether a score separates labeled agents from labeled humans, so it is a natural partner or white-label path. Signals & Standards (launched 9/2026): independent process and claims audit with named personal validation, but no labeled-traffic testing found. They sign process and we supply outcome measurements, so partner or subcontract before competing. Neutronian: supplier-paid certification in ad data, the closest business-model analog. NORC TrueNorth, SSRS Encipher, Ipsos and Verasight: selection-bias calibration or sample, a different problem we no longer touch. ISO 20252/CIRQ and the IA framework: process and self-disclosure, which complement outcome evidence. Vendor in-house red teams are not credible external proof and cannot serve challengers. Edge: neutrality plus ground truth by construction. Both are copyable by DQC or Signals & Standards, so speed and publishing first matter.
result.riskiest_assumption: A paying customer, meaning a challenger detection vendor or a mid-size supplier, will put real money on a labeled-traffic test report from an unknown lab before any end buyer demands such evidence. The seller-pays-referee flows are observed (Dynata to Neutronian, suppliers to CIRQ, P&G's ISO 20252 mandate), but there is no evidence anyone pays for an outcome test. This is the unresolved core of the fatal critique. Secondary risks are the trust cold start for a young founder with no credential, vendor disputes of results (the NSS Labs pattern), and MIT/CloudResearch or DQC commoditizing the benchmark.
result.two_week_test: 14 days, cap about $600. Days 1-4: build a minimal harness with 60 agent sessions (tiers T1-T3, 20 each) and 30 verified humans ($120-200). Host a short survey on the founder's own account and run it through 3-4 tools that offer trials or self-serve access (dtect free 30-day pilot, DQC trial, Prolific/Qualtrics authenticity checks, Verisoul at $99-350 a month, ReDem upload). Touch no production system without consent. Days 5-7: write a two-page teaser, labeled as default trial configuration. Send each tested vendor its own result privately with a 14-day correction window, which doubles as outreach. Days 7-14: send the anonymized teaser to about 40 named targets (challenger vendors, supplier quality leads, agency research directors) and ask for a call. Offer a founder-rate paid pilot with a $1,500 deposit, or a signed LOI naming price and budget owner. PASS: at least 2 deposits or LOIs at $4.5k or more with named budget owners, or 1 deposit plus at least 6 written "would pay $5k or more" from people who name the budget. KILL: 0 deposits and at most 1 "would pay" after at least 10 real conversations, or the harness cannot run labeled sessions through at least 3 tools in 5 days. INCONCLUSIVE: fewer than 10 conversations, so extend one week and do not count it as a pass. If killed, the published benchmark is only a portfolio credential.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed:
The original company is dead and I say so. Critique 2 (fatal) is correct for the buyer-funded audit, and it stays unresolved empirically for the refined version until the 2-week test. I judged it answerable by test, so alive=true is conditional, and the refined idea sits in the lower half on scale and moat.

Critique 1 (serious):
- Asset not scarce, incumbents can add an audit line: conceded. Calibration, the control panel and the "contamination-adjusted estimate" are dropped. The lab owns no sample, so sample owners cannot referee themselves.
- Neutral niche taken and sellers pay referees: adopted. Sell-side payment is the only observed flow, run AV-Comparatives style (public tests free, fees buy services and logo licences, results independent). Partner path with Signals & Standards and DQC.
- Buyers route around an auditor and the audit costs 1-4x the fieldwork bill: conceded. The customer is no longer the buyer, so that ratio no longer applies. Non-consumption (sellers self-test or skip) is still the main competitor and is tested directly.
- Detection half has no pricing power: dropped. We test detectors rather than resell them, and cheap, plentiful detectors raise the need for independent measurement.
- High-stakes wedges lack pull: dropped.

Critique 2 (fatal):
- No proven budget: still true. This is now the single riskiest assumption, with a pre-committed kill.
- Check-signer conflicted or undefined: defined as a challenger-vendor founder or head of product, then a head of quality at a supplier. Conflict is managed by process (vendor-signed config, correction window with no veto, pre-registration, a methodologist co-signer) and is not eliminated.
- White space smaller, scarce asset owned by others: conceded. The mechanism is now injected labeled traffic with no panel dependency.
- Boutique unit economics: accepted. Margins are recomputed, the address-based panel is gone, and the market is resized to $0.15-0.6M realistic.
- Pain solved cheaper or shrinking: partly accepted. Synthetic respondents and direct panels remain tail risks, and the product does not rely on a fraud boom.

Critique 3 (serious):
- TrueNorth, SSRS and Ipsos calibration, and the shaky statistics: conceded and dropped.
- Key input owned by competitors: the lab needs only 100-150 rentable verified humans per test from Prolific, CloudResearch, Verasight or others, so it is fungible and not a dependency.
- Weak why-now and midterm expiry: election hook dropped. Human fraud is old and buyers never paid for it, so the new why-now is self-tested claims, unverified frameworks and cheap attackers.
- Demand unproven and free channels: acknowledged and unresolved until the test.
- Data access and liability: the lab needs no real-panelist paradata because it knows its own labels. Dated measurement reports replace a stamp. NSS Labs-derived safeguards, a liability cap and an E&O quote before the first paid job are required. The credibility cold start is met with pre-registration and a named methodologist, not a reputation.

Remaining unverified: whether DQC or Signals & Standards plan red-team tests, Bot Olympics blue-team details, willingness of any vendor to pay, E&O cost, and supplier counts beyond Cint's self-reported 800+.

result.title: Smoke Report Coverage Matrix
result.one_liner: A 48-hour, per-file triage service that turns carrier-retained smoke/ash/soot hygiene reports into a one-page, source-cited coverage matrix (what was sampled, what was skipped, against what comparator), sold to policyholder-side law firms and public adjusters so they know which files deserve a $2k-$4k CIH second opinion.
result.pitch:
Smoke Report Coverage Matrix is a 48-hour triage service for the lawyers and public adjusters who each hold dozens of Eaton and Palisades smoke files, every one with a carrier-retained hygiene report that nobody has time to read closely. They send the report and lab PDFs. They get back a one-page matrix: how many samples, which media, which zones were sampled or skipped, what comparator was used, the units and detection limits, and internal inconsistencies such as a non-detect result sitting beside a "remediate" recommendation. Each flag cites its source guide, including AIHA's own point that targeted sampling against background is acceptable, and states only what the report did not document. We never label a report inadequate, draft a demand letter, write a sampling plan or give an opinion. The firm's own CIH decides which flagged files deserve a $2,000-$4,000 second opinion, so we make that expert's first hour cheaper and tell the firm where to spend the rest.

What changed from the first pitch: AB 1795 is not proven to reach the 2025 fires, buyers already own a CIH, free tools are coming, and a $395 letter generator sits far above every price anchor. So the price is $95 per file in batches of 50 or more, or $149 for a single PA file, with no subscription, no homeowner tier and no revenue share with experts.

Honest size: roughly $7k-$60k in year one, a 12-18 month window, and no durable moat. It is worth running only because the test is cheap: two real buyers must pay within 14 days.
result.wedge_customer: Primary: policyholder-side coverage and litigation firms with 20+ live Eaton or Palisades standing-home smoke clients (estimated 8-15 firms; includes the class-action and coverage boutiques named in the research). Secondary: public adjuster firms with 10+ disputed smoke files (estimated 10-20 of the 15-25 firms in the zone). Economic buyer is the firm. The user is a paralegal or PA staffer. The validator is the firm's own retained CIH, and 2-3 independent policyholder-side CIHs get the tool free, are paid by the firm at their own rate, and we take no referral fee. result.title: Provider Briefs: Treating-Provider Intelligence for LOP Defense
result.one_liner: A subscription library of source-cited, facts-only briefs on the treating providers behind letter-of-protection injury claims, plus a line-keyed cross outline for each case's bill, sold to Houston then Atlanta defense boutiques out of firm overhead, with no testimony, no signatures and no expert opinions.
result.pitch: Defense lawyers on letter-of-protection injury files do not lack a way to compute a reasonable price. A file-level AI bill audit is now a commodity (CaseMark runs LOP-inflation and benchmark checks in minutes), and any associate can prompt a general LLM for a cross outline. What nobody can prompt is memory across cases: how one surgeon's LOP charges compare with what he submits to Medicare, how often he testifies and for whom, who owns the surgery center, who bought his receivables, what the last depositions looked like. Each boutique sees only its own docket of a provider market that is probably concentrated in a few hundred names per metro (untested). We sell that memory: source-cited, facts-only Provider Briefs plus a line-keyed cross outline for each case's bill, as a monthly subscription that sits in firm overhead like a research seat instead of a case expense that needs carrier pre-approval. First market is Houston, where files and discovery tools exist now; Atlanta follows as Georgia SB 68 files mature in 2027. We deliberately cut what the critics broke: no testimony, no declarations, no signed-expert product, no price arbitrage against $3-5k experts, no "below the approval threshold" hack. Existing coder shops and Georgia experts become referral partners. Bias and billing-practice cross is a lawyer's question, not an expert opinion, so Daubert and AI-declaration rules do not attach. The moat is a cornered resource: a cross-file provider dataset that starts from public records and grows through de-identified, give-to-get contributions. On day one there is no moat, only legwork, and the whole bet is that lawyers will pay card-in-hand for it. The ceiling is small, roughly $0.3-0.6M a year across two metros, with near-zero fixed cost.
result.wedge_customer: A partner (or firm administrator who owns the research-tool budget) at a 3-20 lawyer insurance-defense boutique, Houston first, Atlanta second, who takes carrier-assigned auto and commercial-vehicle bodily-injury files worth $25k-$250k in which a treating provider is on a letter of protection. Not the carrier (a phase-2 buyer only if the test shows carriers will approve), and not experts.
result.first_product: The Provider Brief: a 3-5 page, facts-only, source-cited profile of one named treating provider, clinic or ASC. It holds Medicare Part B submitted-charge vs allowed-amount tables for the provider's top codes where data exist, licence and discipline records, ownership and affiliations from Secretary of State filings, Open Payments, the public litigation footprint (dockets, published rulings, depositions filed as public exhibits), a state-specific discovery checklist (LOP, referral source, factor sale and price, billed vs paid, negotiated rates), and a two-page question bank keyed to the firm's own bill lines (LLM-drafted, human QA). Delivered in 48 hours, concierge by the founder at first, with no patient data in the first two weeks. File-level audit becomes cost of goods, not the product, because CaseMark already sells it cheaply.
result.pricing: All untested guesses that the test is meant to set. $149 per brief, or $349/month per firm (up to 6 briefs plus library search), month to month, $3,490 annual; the first sample brief is free and every later one is paid. This is positioned as firm overhead like a research seat, not a case expense, so it does not depend on carrier reimbursement (the below-pre-approval-threshold claim is dropped; no public threshold exists). Phase 2 only if earned: a carrier or TPA litigation-unit licence of roughly $1.5-3k/month. Testimony and signatures are referred to existing experts for no fee. Cost is 2-3 founder hours per brief now and about $10-20 variable per brief once the library exists (inference).
result.why_now: LLM extraction and public-record synthesis make a source-cited provider brief a few hours of work instead of days, which would not have been true in 2019. But CaseMark shows the file-level audit layer has already collapsed to near-zero price, so the scarce thing moves up to cross-file provider memory. Disclosure regimes generate the facts to collect: Georgia SB 68 (LOP, referral source, receivable sales; causes of action arising on or after 4/21/2025), Texas In re K&L Auto Crushers (discoverable negotiated rates) and Texas 18.001 item-by-item practice. Expert AI-use scrutiny (Kohls v. Ellison and 2026 law-firm guidance) pushes AI away from signed declarations and toward attorney-held work product, which is what this is. Plaintiff AI (EvenUp $2B+, Eve $1B+) raises package polish and volume, but that is context and not proof of defense spend. Honest weaknesses: Georgia volume arrives in 2027, and Texas has no new statute (HB 2446 stalled in the Senate after 5/12/2025, per the bill history I fetched).
result.moat: Primary: cornered resource, a cross-file provider dataset (charges, ownership, testimony history, litigation-derived facts) that no single firm, and no single-file tool like CaseMark, can see. Secondary: switching costs from a firm's saved and annotated briefs, plus a weak give-to-get contribution loop. Reached in stages: month 1 is public data only, which is not a moat; months 3-12 add firm-contributed, de-identified litigation facts; real defensibility needs about 300-500 provider records with at least one litigation-derived fact each, roughly 12-18 months in. Threats: public-only briefs can be copied in a week by a legal-AI vendor, a defense bar could run a free depo bank, carrier SIU data could be shared with panel counsel, and protective orders could block pooling (fallback: public plus firm-owned data only).

result.competitors_and_edge: CaseMark (page fetched): file-level audit of itemized bills against records, UCR/FAIR Health/Medicare fee schedule benchmarks, LOP-inflation and chargemaster-markup analysis, Bates-cited memo in minutes, credit-priced, no expert signature or cross outline named.
